| | Source: [Federal Aviation Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Aviation_Administration "Federal Aviation Administration"),[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-FAA-2) Passenger traffic[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-3) | **Washington Dulles International Airport** ( [_DUL\-iss_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key")) ([IATA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IATA_airport_code "IATA airport code"): **IAD**, [ICAO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ICAO_airport_code "ICAO airport code"): **KIAD**, [FAA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Aviation_Administration "Federal Aviation Administration") [LID](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Location_identifier "Location identifier"): **IAD**) – commonly known simply as **Dulles Airport** – is an [international airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_airport "International airport") serving the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States")'s capital city, [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.") and [its surrounding area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_metropolitan_area "Washington metropolitan area"). It is located 26 miles (42 km) west of [downtown Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_/(Washington,_D.C./) "Downtown (Washington, D.C.)"), in [Loudoun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loudoun_County,_Virginia "Loudoun County, Virginia") and [Fairfax counties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairfax_County,_Virginia "Fairfax County, Virginia") in [Northern Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Virginia "Northern Virginia").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-Facts2-4)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-about-5)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-6) Opened in 1962, the airport is named after [John Foster Dulles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Foster_Dulles "John Foster Dulles"), an influential [secretary of state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_State "United States Secretary of State") during the [Cold War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War "Cold War") who briefly represented [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_/(state/) "New York (state)") in the [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-dedapnv62-7)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-bbupided-8) Operated by the [Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Washington_Airports_Authority "Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority"), Dulles occupies 13,000 acres (20.3 sq mi; 52.6 km2);[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-FAA-2)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-9) IAD ranks third in the United States in terms of land area, after [Denver International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denver_International_Airport "Denver International Airport") and [Dallas Fort Worth International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas_Fort_Worth_International_Airport "Dallas Fort Worth International Airport"). The "striking" and "iconic" [Eero Saarinen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eero_Saarinen "Eero Saarinen")\-designed [Main Terminal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal "Dulles International Airport Main Terminal")[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-10) received vast acclaim for its innovative architecture when it was completed and has gone on to win numerous awards.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-11)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-12)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-13) Dulles is the second busiest of three major airports serving the [Washington–Baltimore metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington%E2%80%93Baltimore_combined_statistical_area "Washington–Baltimore combined statistical area"), behind [Baltimore/Washington International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltimore/Washington_International_Airport "Baltimore/Washington International Airport") (BWI) and ahead of [Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan_Washington_National_Airport "Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport") (DCA).[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-14) As of 2024, it is the [24th-busiest airport in the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_the_busiest_airports_in_the_United_States "List of the busiest airports in the United States"),[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-wapo112714-15) with 27.3 million enplanements.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-:8-16) It had more than 20 million passenger enplanements every year from 2004 to 2019. An average of 60,000 passengers pass through Dulles daily to and from more than 139 destinations around the world.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-traffic_statistics-17)[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-maps-18)[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-19) Dulles has the most international passenger traffic of any airport in the [Mid-Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mid-Atlantic_/(United_States/) "Mid-Atlantic (United States)") outside the [New York metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_metropolitan_area "New York metropolitan area"), including approximately 90% of the international passenger traffic in the Baltimore–Washington region.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-ACI-20) Dulles is a [hub](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airline_hub "Airline hub") for [United Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Airlines "United Airlines"), and it is frequently used by [Star Alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Alliance "Star Alliance") members that United has [codeshare agreements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codeshare_agreement "Codeshare agreement") with. Dulles is also a hub for regional operators [Mesa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesa_Airlines "Mesa Airlines"), [GoJet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GoJet_Airlines "GoJet Airlines"), and [CommuteAir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CommuteAir "CommuteAir"), which operate under the [United Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Express "United Express") brand. Before [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), [Hoover Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoover_Field "Hoover Field") was the main commercial airport serving Washington, on the site now occupied by [the Pentagon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pentagon "The Pentagon") and its parking lots. It was replaced by [Washington National Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan_Washington_National_Airport "Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport") in 1941, a short distance southeast. After the war, in 1948, the [Civil Aeronautics Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_Aeronautics_Administration_/(United_States/) "Civil Aeronautics Administration (United States)") began to consider sites for a second major airport to serve the nation's capital.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-Scheel-21) [Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_United_States_Congress "81st United States Congress") passed the Washington Airport Act in 1950 to provide funding for a new airport in the region.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-22) The initial CAA proposal in 1951 called for the airport to be built in [Fairfax County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairfax_County,_Virginia "Fairfax County, Virginia") near what is now [Burke Lake Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke_Lake_Park "Burke Lake Park"), but protests from residents, as well as the rapid expansion of Washington's suburbs during the time, led to reconsideration of this plan.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-vdh40-23) One competing plan called for the airport to be built in the Pender area of Fairfax County, while another called for the conversion of [Andrews Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrews_Air_Force_Base "Andrews Air Force Base") in [Prince George's County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_George%27s_County,_Maryland "Prince George's County, Maryland"), [Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maryland "Maryland"), into a commercial airport.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-Scheel-21) The current site was selected by President Eisenhower in 1958;[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-vdh40-23) the Dulles name was chosen by Eisenhower's aviation advisor [Pete Quesada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Quesada "Pete Quesada"), who later served as the first head of the [Federal Aviation Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Aviation_Administration "Federal Aviation Administration"). As a result of the site selection, the unincorporated, largely African-American community of [Willard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willard,_Virginia "Willard, Virginia"), which once stood in the airport's current footprint, was demolished, and 87 property owners had their holdings condemned.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-Scheel-21) Dulles was also built over a lesser-known airport named Blue Ridge Airport, chartered in 1938 by the U.S. The airport was Loudoun County's first official airport, consisting of two grass intersecting runways in the shape of an "X". The location of the former Blue Ridge Airport sits where the Dulles Air Freight complex and Washington Dulles Airport Marriott now sit today.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-24)\[_[better source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:NOTRS "Wikipedia:NOTRS")_\] ### Design and construction \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dulles_International_Airport&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: Design and construction")\] [![Image 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/99/Dulles_International_Airport_%281970%29.jpg/250px-Dulles_International_Airport_%281970%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dulles_International_Airport_/(1970/).jpg) Dulles Airport in April 1970, showing the main terminal's original size The civil engineering firm [Ammann and Whitney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ammann_and_Whitney "Ammann and Whitney") was named lead contractor. The airport was dedicated by President [John F. Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy "John F. Kennedy") and Eisenhower on November 17, 1962.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-dedapnv62-7)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-bbupided-8)[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-25) As originally opened, the airport had three long runways (current day runways 1C/19C, 1R/19L, and 12/30) and one shorter one (where current taxiway Q is located). Its original name, Dulles International Airport, was changed in 1984 to Washington Dulles International Airport.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-26) The [main terminal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal "Dulles International Airport Main Terminal") was designed in 1958 by famed Finnish-American architect [Eero Saarinen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eero_Saarinen "Eero Saarinen"), and it is highly regarded for its graceful beauty, suggestive of flight. The terminal was built without any concourses and gates as all aircraft were parked at remote sites. Passengers were bussed to their aircraft by way of mobile lounges that raised up to the aircraft level; some are still in use today. The first midfield terminal that included gates and jetbridges was constructed in 1985 when [New York Air](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Air "New York Air") and other airlines began hub operations at Dulles.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] In the 1990s, the main terminal at Dulles was reconfigured to allow more space between the front of the building and the ticket counters. Additions at both ends of the main terminal more than doubled the structure's length. The original terminal at [Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwan_Taoyuan_International_Airport "Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport") in Taoyuan, Taiwan, was modeled after the Saarinen terminal at Dulles.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-archdaily-27)[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-28) The design included a landscaped man-made lake to collect rainwater, a low-rise hotel, and a row of office buildings along the north side of the main parking lot. The design also included a two-level road in front of the terminal to separate arrival and departure traffic and a federally owned [limited access highway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_Access_Road "Dulles Access Road") connecting the terminal to the Capital Beltway ([I-495](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_495_/(Capital_Beltway/) "Interstate 495 (Capital Beltway)")) about 17 miles (27 km) to the east; the highway system eventually grew to include a parallel toll road to handle commuter traffic and an extension to connect to [I-66](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I-66 "I-66"). The access road had a wide median strip to allow the construction of a passenger rail line, which opened as [an extension of the Washington Metro's Silver Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_Line_/(Washington_Metro/) "Silver Line (Washington Metro)") on November 15, 2022.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-:1-29) By 1985 the original design, featuring [mobile lounges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobile_lounge "Mobile lounge") to meet each plane, was no longer well-suited to Dulles's role as a hub airport. Instead, midfield concourses were constructed to allow passengers to walk between connecting flights without visiting the main terminal. Mobile lounges were still used for international flights and to transport passengers between the midfield concourses and the main terminal; Concourse C/D was the first to be built, followed by Concourse A/B. A tunnel (consisting of a passenger walkway and moving sidewalks) that links the main terminal and Concourse B was opened in 2004.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-walkway-30) The [Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Washington_Airports_Authority "Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority") (MWAA) began a renovation program for the airport including a new security mezzanine with more room for lines.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-Improvement-31) A new train system, dubbed [AeroTrain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AeroTrain_/(Washington_Dulles_International_Airport/) "AeroTrain (Washington Dulles International Airport)") and developed by [Mitsubishi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitsubishi_Heavy_Industries "Mitsubishi Heavy Industries"), began in 2010 to transport passengers between the concourses and the main terminal.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-aerotrain-32) The system, which uses rubber tires and travels along a fixed underground guideway,[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-aerotrain-32) is similar to the people mover systems at [Singapore Changi Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singapore_Changi_Airport "Singapore Changi Airport"),[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-aerotrain-32) [Hartsfield–Jackson Atlanta International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartsfield%E2%80%93Jackson_Atlanta_International_Airport "Hartsfield–Jackson Atlanta International Airport"), and [Denver International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denver_International_Airport "Denver International Airport"). The train is intended to replace the mobile lounges, which many passengers found crowded and inconvenient. The initial phase includes the main terminal station, a permanent Concourse A station, a permanent Concourse B station, a permanent midfield concourse station (with access to the current temporary C concourse via a tunnel with moving walkways), and a maintenance facility.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-aerotrain-32) Mobile lounges continue to serve Concourse D from both the main terminal and Concourse A. Even after AeroTrain is built out and the replacement Concourses C and D are built, the mobile lounges and plane mates will still continue to be used, to transport international arriving passengers to the International Arrivals Building, as well as transport passengers to aircraft parked on hardstands without direct access to jet bridges. Dulles has stated that the wait time for a train does not exceed four minutes, compared to the average 15-minute wait and travel time for mobile lounges.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] Under the development plan, future phases would see the addition of several new midfield concourses and a new south terminal.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-33) A fourth runway (parallel to the existing runways 1 and 19 L&R) opened in 2008,[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-4thRunway-34) and development plans include a fifth runway to parallel the existing runway 12–30.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-5thRunway-35) If this runway is built, the current runway will be re-designated as 12L-30R while the new runway will be designated 12R-30L. An expansion of the B concourse, used by many low-cost airlines as well as international arrivals, has been completed, and the building housing Concourses C and D will eventually be knocked down to make room for a more ergonomic building. Because Concourses C and D are temporary concourses, the only way to get to those concourses is via moving walkway from the Concourse C station, which is built in the location of the future gates and Concourse D by mobile lounge from the main terminal.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-WUSA-36)[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-D2_Project_AeroTrain-37) [![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2d/Escalators_near_departure_zones_3_and_4_at_Dulles_International_Airport.jpg/250px-Escalators_near_departure_zones_3_and_4_at_Dulles_International_Airport.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Escalators_near_departure_zones_3_and_4_at_Dulles_International_Airport.jpg) The interior of the main terminal, showing the escalators leading to baggage claim and arrivals In the short term, [United Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Airlines "United Airlines") has constructed a 20,000 square foot (1,900 m2) buildout on Concourse C between gate C18 and the AeroTrain entrance for use as a Polaris Lounge for international passengers.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-38) Further expansion plans include a new three-story 550,000 square foot (51,000 m2) south concourse building above the AeroTrain station for Concourse C,[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-D2_Project_AeroTrain-37) to replace Concourse A regional gates built in 1999.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-39) Decades-old rules set by Congress that limit the number of takeoffs and landings, as well as distance of routes, at Reagan Airport were intended in part to keep more flights at Dulles. Those rules have been weakened by Congress over the years, however, causing Dulles to lose 200,000 passengers to Reagan between 2011 and 2013.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-wapo112714-15) In 2023, construction started on a 100 MW solar power facility, battery and bus charging equipment.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-40) It would include the largest airport-based solar and battery development in the U.S. as part of an agreement with Dominion Energy. The solar panels would cover more than 835 acres (338 ha) on land, equivalent to the consumption of more than 37,000 Northern Virginia homes during peak production.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-41) ### Operations and milestones \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dulles_International_Airport&action=edit§ion=5 "Edit section: Operations and milestones")\] [![Image 7](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1a/Pat_Nixon_christens_Boeing_747_2749-18.jpg/250px-Pat_Nixon_christens_Boeing_747_2749-18.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pat_Nixon_christens_Boeing_747_2749-18.jpg) First Lady [Pat Nixon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pat_Nixon "Pat Nixon") christening the first [Boeing 747](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_747 "Boeing 747") at Dulles on January 15, 1970. The first scheduled flight at Dulles was an [Eastern Air Lines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Air_Lines "Eastern Air Lines") [Lockheed L-188 Super Electra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_L-188_Electra "Lockheed L-188 Electra") from [Newark International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newark_International_Airport "Newark International Airport") in [New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey "New Jersey") on November 19, 1962.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-Facts-42) The first scheduled transatlantic nonstop flight to serve the airport commenced just shy of two years later, in June 1964.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-43) Dulles was initially considered a [white elephant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_elephant "White elephant"), being far out of town with few flights;[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-daifk-44) in 1965, Dulles averaged 89 airline operations a day while [National Airport (now Reagan)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan_Washington_National_Airport "Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport") averaged 600 despite not allowing jets.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-daifk-44) Airport operations grew along with Virginia suburbs and the [Dulles Technology Corridor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_Technology_Corridor "Dulles Technology Corridor"); perimeter and slot restrictions at National forced long-distance flights to use Dulles. In 1969, Dulles had 2.01 million passengers while National had 9.9 million.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-45) The era of [wide-body jets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wide-body_aircraft "Wide-body aircraft") began on January 15, 1970, when First Lady [Pat Nixon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pat_Nixon "Pat Nixon") christened a [Pan Am](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pan_American_World_Airways "Pan American World Airways") [Boeing 747-100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_747-100 "Boeing 747-100") at Dulles in the presence of Pan Am chairman [Najeeb Halaby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Najeeb_Halaby "Najeeb Halaby").[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-ergpwcgj-46) Rather than a traditional champagne bottle, red, white, and blue water was sprayed on the aircraft.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-pchpln-47) Pan Am's first Boeing 747 flight was from New York–JFK to [London Heathrow Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Heathrow_Airport "London Heathrow Airport").[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-pchpln-47) On December 26, 1973, President Richard Nixon flew from Dulles to Los Angeles on board a United Airlines McDonnell Douglas DC-10 commercial flight instead of on Air Force One. This was due to a nationwide fuel shortage caused at the time by the [Arab oil embargo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973_oil_crisis "1973 oil crisis").[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-48) Less than two years later, on May 24, 1976, supersonic flights between the U.S. and Europe began with the arrival of a [British Airways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Airways "British Airways") [Concorde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concorde "Concorde") from London–Heathrow and an [Air France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_France "Air France") Concorde from [Paris–Charles De Gaulle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_de_Gaulle_Airport "Charles de Gaulle Airport"); both planes were lined nose-to-nose at Dulles for photos.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-ppupi-49)[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-conlands-50)[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-51) On June 12, 1983, the [Space Shuttle _Enterprise_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Enterprise "Space Shuttle Enterprise") arrived at Dulles atop a [modified Boeing 747](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle_Carrier_Aircraft "Shuttle Carrier Aircraft") after touring Europe and before returning to [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base"). Two years later _Enterprise_ returned and was placed in a storage hangar near Runway 12/30 to await construction of a planned [expansion to the National Air and Space Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_F._Udvar-Hazy_Center "Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center"). _Enterprise_ left Dulles on April 27, 2012, for its new home at the [Intrepid Sea, Air & Space Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intrepid_Sea,_Air_%26_Space_Museum "Intrepid Sea, Air & Space Museum") in New York City.[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-intrepid-52) On June 1, 1985, [New York Air](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Air "New York Air") began a small hub operation at Dulles, with 35 daily flights to eight cities in Florida and the northeastern United States.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-:2-53) [Colgan Airways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colgan_Airways "Colgan Airways") became a feeder carrier for New York Air with additional service to smaller cities known as New York Air Connection. In 1987, the airline merged into [Continental Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_Airlines "Continental Airlines"), which maintained the hub operation until 1989.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-:2-53) On October 10, 1985, [Presidential Airways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_Airways_/(scheduled/) "Presidential Airways (scheduled)") opened its hub at the airport, and it soon began a series of code-shares – first with [Pan Am](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pan_Am "Pan Am") from mid-1986 through early 1988, then as [Continental Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_Express "Continental Express") on behalf of [Continental Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_Airlines "Continental Airlines") between mid-1987 and mid-1988, and finally as [United Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Express "United Express"), on behalf of [United Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Airlines "United Airlines"), from mid 1988 until Presidential ceased operations on December 5, 1989.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-54) #### United hub years, 1986 – present \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dulles_International_Airport&action=edit§ion=8 "Edit section: United hub years, 1986 – present")\] On May 1, 1986, [United Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Airlines "United Airlines") began service on 16 new domestic routes creating a hub status at Dulles. Many more domestic routes and new overseas routes would later be added. [Air Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Wisconsin "Air Wisconsin") and Presidential Airways soon became feeder carriers for United operating as [United Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Express "United Express").[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-55) In 1990, a [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") joint resolution to change Dulles International Airport's name to **Washington Eisenhower International Airport** was proposed by [Senator Bob Dole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Dole "Bob Dole"), but the bill did not pass.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-eisenhower-56) When the [SR-71](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SR-71 "SR-71") was retired by the military in 1990, one was flown from its birthplace at United States Air Force [Plant 42](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plant_42 "Plant 42") in [Palmdale, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palmdale,_California "Palmdale, California"), to Dulles, setting a coast-to-coast speed record at an average 2,124 mph (3,418 km/h); the trip took 64 minutes.[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-blackbird-57) The aircraft was placed in a storage building, and is now displayed at the Smithsonian's adjacent [Udvar-Hazy Air and Space Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_F._Udvar-Hazy_Center "Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center").[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-blackbird-57) In 1995, the first flight of the [Boeing 777-200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_777-200 "Boeing 777-200") in commercial service landed at Dulles; the flight was operated by [United Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Airlines "United Airlines") on its transatlantic London Heathrow – Washington Dulles route.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-UAhistory-58) The 2004 launch of [low-cost carrier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low-cost_carrier "Low-cost carrier") [Independence Air](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independence_Air "Independence Air") propelled IAD from being the 24th-busiest airport in the United States to fourth, and one of the top 30 [busiest in the world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World%27s_busiest_airports "World's busiest airports"). Dulles' ranking was an overall 8.22 out of 10.[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-74) Beginning in 2024, an effort by Congress has been made to rename the airport as the Donald J. Trump International Airport, in honor of President [Donald J. Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump").[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-:0-75)[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-:5-76) In April 2024, a bill was proposed in the [United States House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives") to rename the airport after Trump, but did not pass.[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-77)[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-78) A new bill was introduced in the House of Representatives in January 2025, renewing the proposal to rename Dulles after Trump; this bill was announced a few days after a similar state bill was proposed in Tennessee, to rename [Nashville International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nashville_International_Airport "Nashville International Airport") after Trump.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-:0-75)[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-:5-76)[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-79)[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-80) As of February 2025, more than 50 airlines serve the airport.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-81) The majority of the market share is United and United Express while other airlines focus on international routes or domestic routes not served by United. [Airbus A380](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superjumbo "Superjumbo") service to Dulles during the current summer season puts the airport in 3rd place for A380 flights in the US, after [New York–JFK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy_International_Airport "John F. Kennedy International Airport") and [Los Angeles–LAX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_International_Airport "Los Angeles International Airport").[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-82) [British Airways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Airways "British Airways") and [Lufthansa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lufthansa "Lufthansa") fly the superjumbo to Dulles on a daily schedule from May to October, while [Emirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emirates_/(airline/) "Emirates (airline)") flies the A380 year round. Additionally, Dulles is looking to grow its international destinations in response to the regained demand for Southeast Asian service after the pandemic caused numbers to falter significantly. This growth would target cities like [Mumbai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mumbai "Mumbai"), [Taipei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taipei "Taipei") and [Hong Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong "Hong Kong").[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-83) On March 11, 2025, [Air China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_China "Air China") began serving IAD with the [Boeing 747-8i](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_747 "Boeing 747") from [Beijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing_Capital_Airport "Beijing Capital Airport").[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-84) Air China up until then served the airport twice weekly with the [Boeing 777-300ER](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_777 "Boeing 777"). This added a second Air China 747 flight to the US after [JFK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JFK_Airport "JFK Airport"), which had been the only airport in the United States to receive Air China 747 service.[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-85) Dulles originally used **DIA** – the initials of Dulles International Airport – as its airport code.[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-:6-86) When handwritten, DIA was often misread as DCA – the code for Washington National Airport. This prompted officials to change Dulles Airport's code to **IAD** – standing for "International Airport Dulles."[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-:6-86) The airport's terminal complex consists of the **[Main Terminal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal "Dulles International Airport Main Terminal")** (which includes four aircraft gates, known as the **"Z" Gates**), and two parallel midfield terminal buildings: **Concourses A/B** and **Concourses C/D**. The entire terminal complex has a total of 139 [gates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gate_/(airport/) "Gate (airport)") – 123 of which have [jetways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jetways "Jetways") and 16 of which are hardstand locations[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-iad_facts-87) from which passengers can board or disembark using the airport's plane mate vehicles.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-Facts-42) ### Inter-terminal transportation \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dulles_International_Airport&action=edit§ion=12 "Edit section: Inter-terminal transportation")\] [![Image 10](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ef/Dulles_Aerotrain_terminal_B.jpg/250px-Dulles_Aerotrain_terminal_B.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dulles_Aerotrain_terminal_B.jpg) Main Terminal [AeroTrain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AeroTrain_/(Washington_Dulles_International_Airport/) "AeroTrain (Washington Dulles International Airport)") station Conceived in early planning sessions in 1959, Dulles is one of a few remaining airports to utilize [mobile lounges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobile_lounge "Mobile lounge") (also known as "plane mates" or "people movers"), now only used for transport to the International Arrivals Building as well as transport for Concourse D. They have all been given names based on the postal abbreviations of 50 states, e.g., VA, MD, AK.[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-88) The [Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Washington_Airports_Authority "Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority") has partially phased out the mobile lounge system for inter-terminal passenger movements with the [AeroTrain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AeroTrain_/(Washington_Dulles_International_Airport/) "AeroTrain (Washington Dulles International Airport)"), an underground [people mover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People_mover "People mover") that currently operates to all of the concourses except concourse D, with a passenger tunnel remaining to concourses A and B. However, the Aerotrain to concourse C stops at a terminal north of the actual concourse, leaving a significant walk from the terminal to concourse after disembarking. Plane mates remain in use to disembark international passengers and carry them to the International Arrivals Building, as well as to transport passengers to and from aircraft on the hard stands that are called H gates (i.e., those parked remotely on the apron without access to jet bridges).[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-89)[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-90) [![Image 11](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/af/2022-03-24_13_47_19_UTC_minus_4_Ticketing_and_check-in_section_within_the_main_terminal_at_Washington_Dulles_International_Airport_in_the_Dulles_section_of_Sterling%2C_Loudoun_County%2C_Virginia.jpg/250px-thumbnail.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2022-03-24_13_47_19_UTC_minus_4_Ticketing_and_check-in_section_within_the_main_terminal_at_Washington_Dulles_International_Airport_in_the_Dulles_section_of_Sterling,_Loudoun_County,_Virginia.jpg) The Main Terminal's ceiling is suspended in a catenary curve above the check-in area Dulles's main terminal houses ticketing on the upper level, baggage claim and [U.S. Customs and Border Protection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Customs_and_Border_Protection "U.S. Customs and Border Protection") on the lower level, and annexes for the International Arrivals Building for international passenger processing, as well as the four Z gates (used by Air Canada and United Express), H gates, various information kiosks and other support facilities. The main terminal was recognized by the [American Institute of Architects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Institute_of_Architects "American Institute of Architects") in 1966 for its design concept;[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-91) its roof is a [suspended](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suspended_structure "Suspended structure") [catenary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catenary "Catenary") providing a wide enclosed area unimpeded by any columns.[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-Giles_1960-92)[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-Public_Opinion_1961-93) Its main terminal was designed by [Eero Saarinen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eero_Saarinen "Eero Saarinen"), who also designed the [TWA Flight Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TWA_Flight_Center "TWA Flight Center") at [John F. Kennedy International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy_International_Airport "John F. Kennedy International Airport").[\[94\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-94) The main terminal was extended in 1996 to 1,240 feet (380 m)—Saarinen's original design length—which was slightly more than double its originally constructed length of 600 feet (180 m).[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-iad_facts-87) On September 22, 2009, an expansion to include the 41,400 square feet (3,850 m2) International Arrivals Building opened for customs and immigration processing with a capacity to process 2,400 passengers per hour.[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-wp-95) Also in September 2009, a 121,700 square feet (11,310 m2) central [security](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_Security_Administration "Transportation Security Administration") checkpoint was added on a new security mezzanine level of the main terminal. This checkpoint replaced previous checkpoints that were located behind the ticketing areas.[\[96\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-96) Travelers enrolled in [TSA PreCheck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TSA_PreCheck "TSA PreCheck") and [CLEAR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fly_Clear "Fly Clear") still use this area to clear security.[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-97) A separate security checkpoint is available on the baggage claim level for staff only, and previously had access for all passengers as the Dulles Diamond area. Both public security checkpoints connect to escalators to the AeroTrain, which links the main terminal with the A and B concourse and links to a tunnel connecting to the C concourse. All airlines aside from certain express flights operate out of two linear [satellite terminals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satellite_terminal "Satellite terminal"). Each terminal is divided into two concourses, with the north terminal containing Concourses A and B, and the south terminal containing Concourses C and D.[\[98\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-terminal_map-98) [![Image 12](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Dulles_Terminal_-_15.jpg/250px-Dulles_Terminal_-_15.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dulles_Terminal_-_15.jpg) The interior of Concourses A & B. Concourses A and B are located in the midfield terminal building closer to the main terminal. They are utilized by all non-United flights as well as a limited number of [United Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Express "United Express") flights. Concourse A has 47 gates, located in the eastern half of the north midfield terminal. It consists of a permanent ground-level set of gates designed for small planes and United Express flights, and several former Concourse B gates.[\[99\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-99) The concourse is primarily used for international flights. [Air France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_France "Air France") and [KLM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KLM "KLM") have a lounge opposite gate A19, [Etihad Airways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etihad_Airways "Etihad Airways") operates a First and Business Class lounge across from gate A15, and [Virgin Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgin_Atlantic "Virgin Atlantic") has a Clubhouse lounge adjacent to gate A31. Concourse A's AeroTrain station is located between gates A6 and A14.[\[98\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-terminal_map-98) [![Image 13](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c0/KLM_Boeing_787-9_PH-BHE_at_IAD_%2843463954224%29.jpg/250px-KLM_Boeing_787-9_PH-BHE_at_IAD_%2843463954224%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:KLM_Boeing_787-9_PH-BHE_at_IAD_/(43463954224/).jpg) A [KLM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KLM "KLM") [Boeing 787](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_787 "Boeing 787") aircraft serving Terminal A in June 2018. Concourse B has 28 gates, located in the western half of the terminal. It is the first of the permanent elevated midfield concourses. Originally constructed in 1998 and designed by [Skidmore, Owings & Merrill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skidmore,_Owings_%26_Merrill "Skidmore, Owings & Merrill") and [Hellmuth, Obata and Kassabaum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellmuth,_Obata_and_Kassabaum "Hellmuth, Obata and Kassabaum"), the B concourse contained 20 gates. In 2003, 4 additional gates were added, followed by a 15-gate expansion in 2008.[\[100\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-100) In addition to the AeroTrain station located between gates B51 and B62, Concourse B is also connected to the main terminal by an underground walkway. Concourse B is used by some international carriers, and is also utilized by almost all non-United domestic and Canada flights. The facility also includes a [British Airways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Airways "British Airways") Galleries lounge adjacent to the AeroTrain station, a [Lufthansa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lufthansa "Lufthansa") lounge between gates B49 and B51, and a [Turkish Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkish_Airlines "Turkish Airlines") lounge near gate B43.[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-upgrd.com-101) [![Image 14](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/00/KIAD003.jpg/250px-KIAD003.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:KIAD003.jpg) The interior of Concourse C and D, where [United](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Airlines "United Airlines")'s hub operation is based. Concourses C and D are located in the south midfield terminal, and are used for [United Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Airlines "United Airlines") flights, including all mainline flights and most [United Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Express "United Express") regional flights (save for a few that use Concourse A). These concourses were constructed in 1983 as temporary facilities and designed by [Hellmuth, Obata and Kassabaum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellmuth,_Obata_and_Kassabaum "Hellmuth, Obata and Kassabaum"). The two concourses have 22 gates each, numbered C1–C28 and D1–D32, with odd-numbered gates on the north side of the building and even numbered gates on the south side. Concourse C composes the eastern half of the terminal and Concourse D composes the western half.[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-archexp-102)[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-Httpwwwmwaacomdulleshtm-103) The C/D concourses were given a facelift in 2006 that included light-fixture upgrades, new paint finishes, new ceiling grids and tiles, heating and air conditioning replacement, and complete restroom renovations.[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-Httpwwwmwaacomdulleshtm-103) [![Image 15](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e1/United_Airlines_B777-200%2C_N781UA%2C_February_2011%2C_IADairport.jpg/250px-United_Airlines_B777-200%2C_N781UA%2C_February_2011%2C_IADairport.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:United_Airlines_B777-200,_N781UA,_February_2011,_IADairport.jpg) A pair of [United Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Airlines "United Airlines") [Boeing 777-200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_777 "Boeing 777") aircraft at Terminal C in February 2011. While all gates in Concourses C/D can be utilized for both domestic and international departures, all United international arrivals are conducted at gates C1-C14. These gates contain two exit configurations depending on the arriving flight. Domestic passengers and international passengers from airports with [U.S. customs pre-clearance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_border_preclearance "United States border preclearance") exit directly into the concourse, while international arrivals from airports without border pre-clearance are redirected down a sterile corridor to U.S. Customs & Immigration. Passengers arriving from international destinations who are ending their journey at Dulles are then transported by mobile lounge to the International Arrivals Building, while passengers making onward connections are directed to a separate customs facility located on the ground floor of Concourse C. After being screened by TSA at a dedicated security checkpoint within the facility, these passengers then take escalators that deposit them in Concourse C near gate C7.[\[104\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-liveandleftsfly-104) A new and permanent C/D concourse (also called "Tier 2") is planned as part of the D2 Dulles Development Project. The new building is to include a three-level structure with 44 airline gates and similar amenities to Concourse B.[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-Httpwwwmwaacomdulleshtm-103) The concourse plan includes a dedicated mezzanine corridor with moving sidewalks to serve international passengers. The design and construction of the new C/D concourse has not been scheduled.[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-Httpwwwmwaacomdulleshtm-103) When built, it is planned that both terminals will be connected to the main terminal and other concourses via the AeroTrain. To that extent, the AeroTrain station at Concourse C was built at the location where the future Concourse C/D structure is proposed to be built, and is connected to the existing Concourse C via an underground walkway.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-D2_Project_AeroTrain-37) In April 2022, the Airport Authority published plans for a 14 gate Concourse E to be built atop the AeroTrain station with the purpose of replacing outdoor boarding areas at Concourse A. Construction is expected to cost between $500 million and $800 million and the airport is seeking $230 million grants from the Bipartisan Infrastructure Bill.[\[105\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-105) Construction on the concourse began in August 2024, and it is expected to open in 2026.[\[106\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-106) Since many major domestic and international airlines have a large presence at Washington Dulles, there are many airline lounges within the airport: * [Air France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_France "Air France") / [KLM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KLM "KLM"): Air France/KLM Lounge, A Concourse across from gate A22.[\[107\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-mwaa.com-107) * [British Airways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Airways "British Airways"): BA Lounge for First class and Business class passengers (with Concorde Dining offered for First class passengers), located opposite the Concourse B Transit station.[\[108\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-108) * [Capital One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_One "Capital One") opened its second ever airport lounge at Dulles. Ground transportation --------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dulles_International_Airport&action=edit§ion=25 "Edit section: Ground transportation")\] Washington Dulles is accessible via the [Dulles Access Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_Access_Road "Dulles Access Road")/[Dulles Greenway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_Greenway "Dulles Greenway") ([State Route 267](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Route_267_/(Virginia/) "State Route 267 (Virginia)")) and [State Route 28](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Route_28_/(Virginia/) "State Route 28 (Virginia)"). The Access Road is a toll-free, limited access highway owned by the [Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Washington_Airports_Authority "Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority") (MWAA) to facilitate car access to Washington Dulles from the [Capital Beltway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_495_/(Capital_Beltway/) "Interstate 495 (Capital Beltway)") and [Interstate 66](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_66 "Interstate 66").[\[227\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-toll_road-227) After it opened, non-airport traffic between Washington and [Reston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reston,_Virginia "Reston, Virginia") became so heavy that a parallel set of toll lanes were added on the same right-of-way to accommodate non-airport traffic (Dulles Toll Road). The airport-only lanes are both less congested and toll-free. As of November 1, 2008, MWAA assumed responsibility from the [Virginia Department of Transportation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_Department_of_Transportation "Virginia Department of Transportation") both for operating the Dulles Toll Road and for the construction of the [Silver Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_Line_/(Washington_Metro/) "Silver Line (Washington Metro)") down its median. Route 28, which runs north–south along the eastern edge of the airport, has been upgraded to a limited access highway, with the interchanges financed through a property tax surcharge on nearby business properties. The Dulles Toll Road ([VA-267](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_State_Route_267 "Virginia State Route 267")) is extended to the south of [Leesburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leesburg,_Virginia "Leesburg, Virginia") as the Dulles Greenway. ### Public transportation \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dulles_International_Airport&action=edit§ion=27 "Edit section: Public transportation")\] [![Image 36](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1a/Dulles_Airport_Station_Mezzanine_1115.jpg/250px-Dulles_Airport_Station_Mezzanine_1115.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dulles_Airport_Station_Mezzanine_1115.jpg) The [Dulles Airport Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_station "Dulles International Airport station") of the [Washington Metro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Metro "Washington Metro") is part of the system's [Silver Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_Line_/(Washington_Metro/) "Silver Line (Washington Metro)"). [Washington Metro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Metro "Washington Metro") service is available to Dulles via the [station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_station "Dulles International Airport station") on the [Silver Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_Line_/(Washington_Metro/) "Silver Line (Washington Metro)").[\[228\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-Dulles_Metro-228) Service began operation on November 15, 2022.[\[229\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-229) [Fairfax Connector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairfax_Connector "Fairfax Connector") bus routes 952 (to [Herndon station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herndon_station "Herndon station"), [Reston Town Center station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reston_Town_Center_station "Reston Town Center station"), and [Wiehle–Reston East station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiehle%E2%80%93Reston_East_station "Wiehle–Reston East station") via [Sunset Hills Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sunset_Hills_Road&action=edit&redlink=1 "Sunset Hills Road (page does not exist)")) and 983 (to [Innovation Center station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Innovation_Center_station "Innovation Center station") and [Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_F._Udvar-Hazy_Center "Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center")) serve Washington Dulles at the Kiss and Fly near the airport Metro station (moved from a terminal-adjacent stop in November 2025).[\[230\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-ffx-bus-952-230)[\[231\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-ffx-bus-983-231)[\[232\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-232) Formerly, the [Metrobus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metrobus_/(Washington,_D.C./) "Metrobus (Washington, D.C.)") [5A route](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D.C.%E2%80%93Dulles_Line "D.C.–Dulles Line") served the airport. [Megabus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megabus_/(North_America/) "Megabus (North America)") provides service from Dulles to [Charlottesville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlottesville,_Virginia "Charlottesville, Virginia") and [Blacksburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blacksburg,_Virginia "Blacksburg, Virginia"). Washington Flyer has a [monopoly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monopoly "Monopoly") to operate cabs from Washington Dulles Airport.[\[233\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-233) [Uber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uber "Uber") and [Lyft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyft "Lyft") are popular modes of transport to and from the airport, and MWAA receives a $4 fee per trip, which is included in the quoted fare.[\[234\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-234) Accidents and incidents ----------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dulles_International_Airport&action=edit§ion=28 "Edit section: Accidents and incidents")\] [![Image 37](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/IAD_ATCT.jpg/250px-IAD_ATCT.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:IAD_ATCT.jpg) Control tower view of IAD in 1961 * On October 1, 1965, a [Cessna 182](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cessna_182 "Cessna 182") crashed on approach to Dulles Airport in a field in [Chantilly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chantilly,_Virginia "Chantilly, Virginia"), killing all four occupants on board.[\[235\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-235)[\[236\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-236) * There were three deaths during a nine-day air show held at Washington Dulles in conjunction with Transpo '72 (officially called the U.S. International Transportation Exposition, a $10 million event sponsored by the U.S. Department of Transportation, and attended by over one million visitors from around the world). * On May 29, 1972, the third day of the show, the pilot of a Kite Rider (a variety of hang glider) was killed in a crash. This was to be the first of the three air deaths during the Air Show.[\[237\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-rickpowell_1-237)[\[238\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-238) * On June 3, 1972, a second death occurred at the Transpo '72 Air Show, during a sport plane pylon race. At 2:40 pm, during the second lap and near a turn about pylon 3, a trailing aircraft's (LOWERS R-1 N66AN) wing and propeller hit the right wing tip of a leading aircraft (CASSUTT BARTH N7017). The right wing immediately sheared off the fuselage, and the damaged aircraft crashed almost instantly, killing the 29-year-old pilot, Hugh C. Alexander. He was a professional Air Racer with over 10,200 hours.[\[239\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-rickpowell_2-239)[\[240\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport#cite_note-rickpowell_3-240) * On June 4, 1972, during the last day of the 9-day Transpo '72 Air Show, the U.S. Air Force Thunderbirds experienced their first fatal crash at an air show. Major Joe Howard flying Thunderbird 3 was killed when his F-4E-32-MC Phantom II, 66-0321, lost power during a vertical maneuver. The pilot broke out of formation just after he completed a wedge roll and was ascending at around 2,500 feet (760 m) AGL. The aircraft staggered and descended in a flat attitude with little forward speed. Although Major Howard ejected as the aircraft fell back to earth from about 1,500 feet (460 m) tail first, and descended under a good canopy, winds blew him into the fireball ascending from the blazing crash site. The Metrorail station at Dulles International Airport is connected to the main terminal by an indoor pedestrian tunnel with moving sidewalks.

*   The tunnel provides convenient access to the airport’s ticketing and baggage claim levels. 
*   Signs guide customers to the tunnel, which also links the terminal with **Parking Garage 1**. 
*   Passengers are advised to consult [Metrorail’s website](https://www.wmata.com/rider-guide/silver-line-extension/Washington-Dulles-International-Airport.cfm) for station information, train service advisories, fares and operating hours. 
*   The station services the **Silver Line**. For more information, here is the [metro system map](https://chrome-extension//efaidnbmnnnibpcajpcglclefindmkaj/https://www.wmata.com/schedules/maps/upload/system-map-rail.pdf).

###### [Tap. Ride. Go. - Just tap your preferred card to ride](https://www.wmata.com/fares/how-to-pay/tap-ride-go.cfm)

Passengers can now “Tap. Ride. Go.” with contactless credit, debit cards at Metrorail station faregates.

How to Use Tap. Ride. Go.

*   Select your contactless credit or debit card contactless symbol (physical card or mobile wallet).
*   Tap your card or device at any Metrorail faregate to enter a station.
*   Tap your same card or device at any Metrorail faregate to exit a station.

**Architects:** Eero Saarinen  
**Year:** 1962  
**Photographs:** MWAA, Laughing Squid, askpang, architecture-history.org  
**Manufacturers:** Security Metal Products Corp  
**Country:** United States

Dulles International Airport terminal building designed by Eero Saarinen and Associates in Willard, Virginia, redefined American airport architecture upon its 1962 completion as the first facility purpose-built for jet aircraft. Commissioned by the Civil Aeronautics Authority and selected under President Eisenhower in 1958, the airport honored Secretary of State John Foster Dulles and embodied Cold War-era infrastructural ambition. Saarinen, supported by Ammann and Whitney and consultant Charles Landrum, developed a design rooted in data-driven passenger flow analysis, leading to the introduction of mobile lounges that eliminated the need for fixed concourses. The 15-bay modular terminal, later expanded in 1997, features a cable-supported roof suspended from outward-sloping concrete piers—described by Saarinen as “a huge continuous hammock suspended between concrete trees.” Positioned atop a vertically zoned roadway system, the terminal asserts a monumental civic identity, earning comparisons to a “Jet-Age Parthenon.” Saarinen’s expressive vocabulary references earlier works like the Ingalls Hockey Rink and resonates with expressionist architecture, influencing future terminals by Renzo Piano and Santiago Calatrava. Dulles International Airport remains both a functional hub and a lasting symbol of postwar American design, serving over 23 million passengers and 125 destinations annually.

![Image 1: Dulles international airport / eero saarinen | classics on architecture lab](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-20.jpg)

Dulles International Airport, situated 28 miles (45 kilometers) southwest of Washington, D.C., was conceived as the international gateway to the U.S. capital. Selected in 1958 by President Dwight D. Eisenhower, the site near the small town of Willard in Virginia became the location for the first American airport specifically designed to accommodate jet aircraft. The facility was named after Secretary of State John Foster Dulles, a key figure in Cold War diplomacy who passed away in 1959.

![Image 2: Dulles international airport / eero saarinen | classics on architecture lab](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-77.jpg)

Commissioned by the Civil Aeronautics Authority (CAA), [Eero Saarinen](https://www.architecturelab.net/architect/famous/eero-saarinen/) and Associates were tasked with designing the airport. Saarinen envisioned an architecture that embodied the grace and dynamism of flight while serving the growing operational demands of jet travel. The architectural and engineering team included Ammann and Whitney, while the airport consultant was Charles Landrum. Following Saarinen’s death in 1961, the project was completed under the supervision of his associates Kevin Roche and John Dinkeloo.

[![Image 3: Dulles international airport / eero saarinen | classics on architecture lab](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-112-1140x858.jpg)](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-112-scaled.jpg)

Dulles International Airport / Eero Saarinen | Classics on Architecture Lab 137

[![Image 4: Dulles international airport / eero saarinen | classics on architecture lab](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-71-707x1024.jpg)](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-71.jpg)

Dulles International Airport / Eero Saarinen | Classics on Architecture Lab 138

[![Image 5: Dulles international airport / eero saarinen | classics on architecture lab](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-73-685x1024.jpg)](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-73.jpg)

Dulles International Airport / Eero Saarinen | Classics on Architecture Lab 139

[![Image 6: Dulles international airport / eero saarinen | classics on architecture lab](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-66-1008x1024.jpg)](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-66.jpg)

Dulles International Airport / Eero Saarinen | Classics on Architecture Lab 140

[![Image 7: Dulles international airport / eero saarinen | classics on architecture lab](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-95-1009x1024.jpg)](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-95.jpg)

Dulles International Airport / Eero Saarinen | Classics on Architecture Lab 141

The original terminal, completed in 1962, introduced several pioneering concepts in airport design. Among the most distinctive was the use of mobile lounges—self-powered passenger transporters that ferried travelers directly from the main terminal to aircraft parked away from the building. This eliminated the need for traditional finger-like concourses and allowed for flexible aircraft positioning. Though the concept was never widely adopted, these vehicles remain in use at Dulles, now supplemented by fixed concourses added in later expansions.

[![Image 8: Dulles international airport / eero saarinen | classics on architecture lab](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-78-1007x1024.jpg)](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-78.jpg)

Dulles International Airport / Eero Saarinen | Classics on Architecture Lab 142

[![Image 9: Dulles international airport / eero saarinen | classics on architecture lab](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-53-1140x791.jpg)](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-53-scaled.jpg)

Dulles International Airport / Eero Saarinen | Classics on Architecture Lab 143

[![Image 10: Dulles international airport / eero saarinen | classics on architecture lab](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-76-1022x1024.jpg)](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-76.jpg)

Dulles International Airport / Eero Saarinen | Classics on Architecture Lab 144

[![Image 11: Dulles international airport / eero saarinen | classics on architecture lab](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-54-1140x775.jpg)](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-54-scaled.jpg)

Dulles International Airport / Eero Saarinen | Classics on Architecture Lab 145

Saarinen approached the project with a methodical design process. For over a year, the team studied passenger flow at airports across the country. Staffers were instructed to time every step of their own travel experiences, with Saarinen himself famously using a stopwatch during trips. The data collected helped develop a streamlined operational model centered around the mobile lounge system and a single, monumental terminal. To help communicate this unfamiliar concept, Saarinen invited Charles and Ray Eames to create a short film titled The Expanding Airport. While airline executives were skeptical, the CAA supported the proposal after realizing a conventional terminal with similar capacity would require concourses extending over 8,000 feet (2,438 meters). The resulting main terminal structure is both functional and expressive. Saarinen designed it as a pavilion composed of 15 modular bays, each 40 feet (12 meters) wide, which allowed for straightforward expansion. In fact, in 1997, the terminal was doubled in length with 300-foot (91-meter) extensions at both ends, following the original modular logic.

![Image 12: Dulles international airport / eero saarinen | classics on architecture lab](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-16.jpg)

Structurally, the terminal’s form relies on a set of bold engineering gestures. The roof, celebrated for its upward sweep, is suspended by cables strung between rows of monumental concrete piers. These piers rise 65 feet (20 meters) along the landside façade, then descend to 40 feet (12 meters) airside, framing a canopy for the mobile lounges. Saarinen described the roof as “like a huge continuous hammock suspended between concrete trees,” with the poured-in-place slabs inserted between the cable supports. The piers slant outward from each side, a move both functional—balancing the cable tension—and expressive, giving the terminal a soaring and dynamic quality. Saarinen admitted: “We exaggerated and dramatized this outward slope to give the colonnade a dynamic and soaring look as well as a stately and dignified one.” This deliberate fusion of modern engineering and classical gesture connected Dulles to Washington’s neoclassical architectural tradition while asserting its own identity as a symbol of the jet age. Saarinen referred to it as “the best thing I have done…. Maybe it will even explain what I believe about architecture.”

[![Image 13: Dulles international airport / eero saarinen | classics on architecture lab](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-38-1140x780.jpg)](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-38-scaled.jpg)

Dulles International Airport / Eero Saarinen | Classics on Architecture Lab 146

[![Image 14: Dulles international airport / eero saarinen | classics on architecture lab](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-62-1140x727.jpg)](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-62-scaled.jpg)

Dulles International Airport / Eero Saarinen | Classics on Architecture Lab 147

[![Image 15: Dulles international airport / eero saarinen | classics on architecture lab](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-37-1140x756.jpg)](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-37-scaled.jpg)

Dulles International Airport / Eero Saarinen | Classics on Architecture Lab 148

[![Image 16: Dulles international airport / eero saarinen | classics on architecture lab](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-6-1140x780.jpg)](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-6.jpg)

Dulles International Airport / Eero Saarinen | Classics on Architecture Lab 149

[![Image 17: Dulles international airport / eero saarinen | classics on architecture lab](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-28-1140x760.jpg)](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-28.jpg)

Dulles International Airport / Eero Saarinen | Classics on Architecture Lab 150

Approached by automobile, the building sits elevated atop a layered roadway system that separates arrival, departure, and parking flows. This vertical zoning enhances the clarity of vehicular movement while reinforcing the temple-like presentation of the terminal. Critics and admirers alike have likened the pavilion to a “Jet-Age Parthenon” resting atop a modern Acropolis.

[![Image 18: Dulles international airport / eero saarinen | classics on architecture lab](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-27-1140x765.jpg)](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-27.jpg)

Dulles International Airport / Eero Saarinen | Classics on Architecture Lab 151

[![Image 19: Dulles international airport / eero saarinen | classics on architecture lab](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-92-792x1024.jpg)](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-92.jpg)

Dulles International Airport / Eero Saarinen | Classics on Architecture Lab 152

[![Image 20: Dulles international airport / eero saarinen | classics on architecture lab](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-107-1140x805.jpg)](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-107.jpg)

Dulles International Airport / Eero Saarinen | Classics on Architecture Lab 153

[![Image 21: Dulles international airport / eero saarinen | classics on architecture lab](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-99-1119x1024.jpg)](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-99.jpg)

Dulles International Airport / Eero Saarinen | Classics on Architecture Lab 154

The roof’s lineage can be traced to Saarinen’s earlier work on the Ingalls Hockey Rink (1959) at Yale University, another cable-supported structure. The dramatic roof profile and the expressive use of concrete have also drawn comparisons to Erich Mendelsohn’s early expressionist sketches. In the years since its completion, Dulles has become an icon of American postwar architecture, featured in films such as Seven Days in May (1964), Die Hard 2, The X-Files, and Forces of Nature. The airport has also served as inspiration for later terminal designs, including Renzo Piano’s Kansai International Airport in Osaka and [Santiago Calatrava](https://www.architecturelab.net/architect/famous/santiago-calatrava/)’s design for Bilbao.

[![Image 22: Dulles international airport / eero saarinen | classics on architecture lab](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-38-1140x780.jpg)](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-38-scaled.jpg)

Dulles International Airport / Eero Saarinen | Classics on Architecture Lab 155

[![Image 23: Dulles international airport / eero saarinen | classics on architecture lab](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-6-1140x780.jpg)](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-6.jpg)

Dulles International Airport / Eero Saarinen | Classics on Architecture Lab 156

[![Image 24: Dulles international airport / eero saarinen | classics on architecture lab](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-90-683x1024.jpg)](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-90.jpg)

Dulles International Airport / Eero Saarinen | Classics on Architecture Lab 157

Today, Dulles remains a major international hub, handling over 23 million passengers per year and serving more than 125 destinations. Its architectural legacy endures not only in its physical presence but in its broader impact on transportation architecture. Like his father Eliel Saarinen’s Helsinki Central Station, Eero Saarinen’s Dulles terminal stands as a masterwork of its type, elevating infrastructure into cultural form.

![Image 25: Dulles international airport / eero saarinen | classics on architecture lab](https://www.architecturelab.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/dulles-international-airport-eero-saarinen-24.jpg)
