**FAA’s “White Elephant”**

**Theresa L. Kraus, FAA Historian**

On November 17, 1962, ceremonies marked the opening of FAA’s Dulles International Airport
(renamed Washington Dulles International Airport in 1984). President John F. Kennedy
officially dedicated the airport, named for the late Secretary of State John Foster Dulles, with
former President Dwight D. Eisenhower in attendance. Other dignitaries celebrating the opening
included FAA Administrator Najeeb Halaby, Mrs. John Foster Dulles, and former CIA Director

Alan Dulles, brother of John Foster Dulles.

![](https://wy-static.wenxiaobai.com/11038818215920457869/11038818215920457869.pdf-0-0.png)


The second airport owned and operated by the FAA, Dulles was the first U.S. airport specifically
designed to handle jet aircraft. The opening ceremonies came after 12 long years of planning,
controversy, and construction. With capacity at its limit at Washington National Airport after
World War II, the CAA, Congress, and the White House began contemplating construction of a
second airport to serve the region. President Truman signed Public Law 762 on September 7,
1950, which directed the Secretary of Commerce (to whom the CAA reported) "to construct,
protect, operate, improve, and maintain" a second public airport for the Washington, DC, area.
The act authorized appropriations not to exceed $14 million, and Congress subsequently
authorized $1 million to launch the project.


After considering several sites in Maryland and Virginia, the CAA decided to locate the new
airport in Burke, VA. By the end of 1951, 1,046 of the required 4,570 acres had been purchased


at the Burke location. When local opposition to the project developed, however, Congress
refused to appropriate additional funds.


From 1953-1955, CAA conducted a number of studies to determine the best alternative to the

Burke site. In December 1955, following Senate hearings in July, the CAA reiterated its earlier
position that the Maryland site occupied by Andrews Air Force Base would be the best location,
but again recommended Burke as the next best alternative. Congress turned down a request for
$34.7 million to complete the Burke project when strong opposition to that site continued at
Senate hearings in July 1956.


The following year, in August 1957, Congress appropriated $12.5 million for a second airport for
Washington, DC, to be built on a site to be recommended by President Eisenhower. The
President charged his special assistant for aviation, General Elwood “Pete” Quesada with site
selection. In a report to Congress on January 16, 1958, President Eisenhower endorsed
Quesada’s recommendation to build the airport at Chantilly, VA. Many local residents and many
in the aviation community disagreed with the decision. They called the new airport a “white
elephant,” claiming it a waste of tax payer money because no one would use the airport since it
was so far from Washington, DC.


Land acquisition began on January 27, 1958, after condemnation proceedings by the Department
of Justice. With land acquisition and projected construction costs rising, on July 11, 1958,
Congress removed the ceiling of $14 million for construction. On August 1, the U.S.
Government took official possession of the original 8,200-acre Washington international airport
site at Chantilly. Construction on what was eventually to become Dulles International Airport
began the following month, on September 2.


To clear the airport land, construction workers tore down 580 buildings, including 300 homes,
closed 15 miles of secondary roads, excavated 12 million cubic yards of earth, and built the
world’s largest concrete plant on site. The plant ultimately used more than 250,000 tons of sand,
600,000 tons of crushed stone, and 750,000 barrels of cement. By the end of construction,
workers poured approximately 1.2 million cubic yards of Portland cement, not counting an
estimated half-million square yards of asphaltic concrete for the runway shoulders.


CAA’s successor organization, FAA contracted with renowned
architect Eero Saarinen to design the terminal building. The design
was radically different from contemporary terminals. By eliminating
the “fingers” or spokes that spread out from other terminals to
accommodate arriving and departing aircraft, Saarinen designed the
Dulles terminal as a sleek, two-story building, 600 feet long and 150

feet wide.


Saarinen referred to the terminal as “the best thing I have done.” His
Terminal under construction design won one of three "first honors" awards for architectural



![](https://wy-static.wenxiaobai.com/11038818215920457869/11038818215920457869.pdf-1-0.png)
excellence presented by the American Institute of Architects in 1966. The awards jury cited the
terminal for conveying the "free and graceful movement that we associate with flight," and stated
that the entire project set "a new high in architectural achievement by the Federal Government."
In May 1978, the terminal was listed on the National Register of Historic Places.


With no “finger” ramp areas, FAA contracted for a fleet of mobile lounges to carry passengers
from the terminal to their departing planes or from arriving planes to the terminal. The mobile
lounges, designed and built by the Chrysler Corporation Defense Operations Division and the
Budd Company, were the largest passenger carrying vehicles ever built to be operated on rubber
tires. At 54 feet long, 17 ½ feet high, and 16 feet wide, they compared in size to 8 intercity buses
arranged with two side by side, two more parked to the rear of those, and four more stacked on
top of each of the first four.


The new airport opened for training and
familiarization flights on October 1, 1962. After the
formal dedication ceremony on November 17, it
opened for commercial traffic on November 19. The
first airlines to fly into Dulles on that day were

Braniff, Delta, Eastern, Northwest, and TWA.



![](https://wy-static.wenxiaobai.com/11038818215920457869/11038818215920457869.pdf-2-0.png)

at the dedication ceremony



Dulles’ original identifier was DIA. Because of
passenger confusion between Dulles and the Dallas
airport, including a number of people ending up at
the wrong destination, FAA changed the identifier
to IAD on May 22, 1968.

The **Dulles International Airport Main Terminal** is located in [Loudoun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loudoun_County,_Virginia "Loudoun County, Virginia") and [Fairfax counties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairfax_County,_Virginia "Fairfax County, Virginia") in [Dulles, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles,_Virginia "Dulles, Virginia"), United States. The original structure, 600 feet (180 m) long and 150 feet (46 m) wide, was designed by [Eero Saarinen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eero_Saarinen "Eero Saarinen") and completed in 1962 as the first terminal at [Dulles International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport "Dulles International Airport"). Annexes to the west and east were completed in 1996 as part of a renovation designed by [Skidmore, Owings & Merrill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skidmore,_Owings_%26_Merrill "Skidmore, Owings & Merrill") (SOM), bringing its total length to 1,240 feet (380 m). The terminal is operated by the [Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Washington_Airports_Authority "Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority"), which operates Dulles Airport as a whole. The terminal's design is a [suspended structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suspended_structure "Suspended structure") with roof panels of precast concrete suspended between cables which span the width of the building.

The Main Terminal's design includes parallel slanted [colonnades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonnade "Colonnade") on the terminal's north and south facades, interspersed with glass walls. The [landside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landside "Landside") facade to the north is taller than the [airside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airside "Airside") facade to the south; a concave roof supported by cables connects the two facades, descending toward the center. A concourse and [control tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Control_tower "Control tower") extend south toward the airport's [apron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airport_apron "Airport apron"). The interior was originally divided into two levels: an upper story for departing passengers and a lower story for arriving passengers. Saarinen's original design included [mobile lounges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobile_lounge "Mobile lounge") that ferried passengers directly to planes, reducing the need for long walks or [taxiing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxiing "Taxiing") while increasing the airport's operational flexibility. The modern terminal includes four [airline gates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gate_/(airport/) "Gate (airport)") known as Z gates, where aircraft could unload passengers directly. In addition, two basements contain security screening facilities and an [AeroTrain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AeroTrain_/(Dulles_International_Airport/) "AeroTrain (Dulles International Airport)") people-mover station.

The 1950 Washington Airport Act provided funding for Dulles Airport, land for which was acquired in January 1958. Saarinen was selected that May to design the terminal, construction of which began in early 1960. After several delays, the terminal was dedicated on November 17, 1962, along with the rest of the airport. Initially, Dulles Airport saw lower-than-expected usage, but increased patronage prompted the airport's original operator, the [Federal Aviation Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Aviation_Administration "Federal Aviation Administration") (FAA), to contemplate an expansion in the early 1970s. [Hellmuth, Obata & Kassabaum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HOK_/(firm/) "HOK (firm)") (HOK) built two small annexes to the south in 1978, and further expansions and additional terminals were contemplated in the 1980s following increases in patronage. SOM designed annexes to the west and east, which began construction in October 1993 and were dedicated on September 6, 1996. Additional expansions took place in the 2000s, including the Z gates and the basements.

The structure was widely acclaimed when it was completed, particularly regarding its shape; Saarinen reportedly considered it his best work. The terminal has received numerous awards, including the [American Institute of Architects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Institute_of_Architects "American Institute of Architects")' [Twenty-five Year Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twenty-five_Year_Award "Twenty-five Year Award"), and other terminal buildings have been compared with it. Though the Main Terminal was nominated for inclusion on the [National Register of Historic Places](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Register_of_Historic_Places "National Register of Historic Places") in 1978, it was never added due to objections from the FAA.

The Main Terminal of [Dulles International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport "Dulles International Airport") is in [Dulles, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles,_Virginia "Dulles, Virginia"), United States, some 26 to 27 miles (42 to 43 km) from Washington, D.C.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Mehaffy_p._S4-1)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Haughland_1962-2)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Boston_Globe_1962-3)[\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-5) The airport, serving the [Washington metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_metropolitan_area "Washington metropolitan area"), straddles the border between [Loudoun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loudoun_County,_Virginia "Loudoun County, Virginia") and [Fairfax counties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairfax_County,_Virginia "Fairfax County, Virginia").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-6) The terminal is placed between Dulles Airport's original north–south runways.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Hailey_1960-7)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Stroud_p._558-8) It is one of several terminal structures at Dulles Airport, along with several outlying "midfield concourses" and the International Arrivals Building,[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-flydulles.com_1962-9)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Mehaffy_p._S5-10) all of which were developed after the original terminal.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Mehaffy_p._S5-10)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-11) The terminal was built to smaller dimensions than comparable terminals at other airports because it used [mobile lounges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobile_lounge "Mobile lounge"), which transported passengers from the terminal to planes[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-McLeod_1959-12)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Merkel_p._219-13)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Armstrong_1960-14) and, later, to the concourses.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Schwartz_p._50-15)[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Field_1999-16)

The original terminal was designed in a [mid-century modern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mid-century_modern "Mid-century modern") style by [Eero Saarinen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eero_Saarinen "Eero Saarinen")[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-17)[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-18) and was his only work in Virginia.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-19) Saarinen worked with structural engineering firm [Ammann & Whitney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ammann_%26_Whitney "Ammann & Whitney"), mechanical engineering firm [Burns & McDonnell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burns_%26_McDonnell "Burns & McDonnell"), and airport consultant Charles Landrum.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Merkel_p._216-20)[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-AF_p._82-21)[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Roman_p._116-22) The Corbetta Construction Company was the main contractor,[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-AF_p._82-21)[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Hailey_1960a-23) while Humphreys & Harding installed the finishes.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-AF_p._82-21) Other figures involved in the building's construction included lighting consultant [Richard Kelly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Kelly_/(lighting_designer/) "Richard Kelly (lighting designer)") and landscape designer [Dan Kiley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Kiley "Dan Kiley").[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-AF_p._82-21) The Main Terminal was intended to symbolize the [Jet Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jet_Age "Jet Age")[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_Times_1960-24)[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Roman_p._117-25) and, from the outset, was designed with future expansions in mind.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-A-1988-05-26) Saarinen described his design as a "huge continuous hammock suspended between concrete trees",[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Kenworthy_n797-27)[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Kohlmeier_1962-28) saying it represented a solution for what to put "between earth and sky".[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Sehlstedt_1962a-29)[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Roman_p._117-25) The western and eastern annexes were designed by [David Childs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Childs "David Childs"), Michael McCarthy, and Marilyn Taylor of [Skidmore, Owings and Merrill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skidmore,_Owings_and_Merrill "Skidmore, Owings and Merrill") (SOM) in a similar style to the original building.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Arch_p._40-30) Ammann & Whitney was also the engineer for SOM's expansion.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Arch_p._40-30)[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Freeman_p._63-31)

[![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/21/Airport_Washington_Dulles_05.jpg/250px-Airport_Washington_Dulles_05.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Airport_Washington_Dulles_05.jpg)

View from the south (2020)

The original terminal measured 600 feet (180 m) long and 150 feet (46 m) wide.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Stroud_p._558-8)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Merkel_p._219-13)[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Jones_1962-32)[\[b\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-33) Both ends were built with provisions for extensions measuring 300 feet (90 m) long,[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Merkel_p._219-13)[\[c\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-34) for a total length of 1,200 feet (370 m).[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_Times_1960-24)[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Kenworthy_n797-27) The base of the original terminal, including vehicular ramps, was intended to support such an expansion,[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Ames_v927-35)[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Freeman_p._67-36) which was intended to have the same cross-section as the original terminal.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-37) In particular, the vehicular ramps paralleled the terminal for its entire proposed length, and Saarinen added empty openings at the terminal's base to accommodate future entrances.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Freeman_p._67-36) When the annexes were eventually built in the 1990s, they were 320 feet (98 m) long,[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Reingold_1994-38)[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Cullerton_1996-39)[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_Times-Tribune_1996-40) giving the terminal a total length of 1,240 feet (380 m).[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Reid_1996-41) Just west of the Main Terminal is the International Arrivals Terminal, which abuts the Main Terminal's base.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Freeman_p._67-36)

The vehicular drop-off and pick-up ramps are on the north, or [landside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landside "Landside"), facade of the terminal;[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Giles_1960-42) there were originally separate loading bays for taxis, private vehicles, and buses or limousines.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Ashton_1961-43) The ramps loop around a parking area nicknamed the "bowl",[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-44) while later parking garages were built away from the terminal to preserve views of the building.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Civil_Engineering_2000-45) The ramps are reached by the [Dulles Access Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_Access_Road "Dulles Access Road"), which leads east toward Washington, D.C.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Jones_1962-32)[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Kohlmeier_1962-28) The Dulles Access Road, the airport's original main approach road, was intended as a major part of the terminal's design, providing passengers views of the building as it emerged from the landscape;[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Mehaffy_p._4.8-46) it was landscaped by Kiley.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Freeman_p._63-31) Plans for a [Washington Metro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Metro "Washington Metro") line to serve the terminal had been considered since the 1960s,[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-47) though the [Dulles International Airport station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_station "Dulles International Airport station") did not open until 2022.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-48) A 1996 expansion to the original terminal contained provisions for connections to a future Metro station.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Reid_1996-41)[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-49)

Along the terminal's south or [airside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airside "Airside") facade, a concourse extends southward.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Stroud_p._558-8) Initially, the southern facade had loading docks for 24 mobile lounges,[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Jones_1962-32) with 12 on either side of the south concourse.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Stroud_p._558-8) There is a 177-foot-tall (54 m)[\[d\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-51) [airport control tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airport_control_tower "Airport control tower") above the south concourse.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Jones_1962-32)[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-52)[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Rife_1968-53) The tower itself is 160 feet (49 m) tall and is topped by a [radome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radome "Radome") measuring 17 feet (5.2 m) in diameter; the tower was decommissioned in 2007 but remains in place.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Kelly_j193-54) The Main Terminal also has four gates known as the Z gates, where aircraft can load and unload passengers directly;[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-flydulles.com_1962-9) these are located along the southern facade, east of the south concourse.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Schwartz_p._52-55) South of the terminal is the airport's [apron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airport_apron "Airport apron").[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Hailey_1960b-56)

[![Image 4](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2e/Dulles_Terminal_-_2.jpg/250px-Dulles_Terminal_-_2.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dulles_Terminal_-_2.jpg)

Exterior view of the northern (landside) colonnade of the terminal (2023)

The concave roof is supported by two parallel [colonnades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonnade "Colonnade") to the north and south, which divide each facade into [bays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_/(architecture/) "Bay (architecture)") measuring 40 feet (12 m) wide. In the original portion of the terminal, there are 16 columns in each colonnade.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Jones_1962-32)[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Ashton_1961-43) The northern colonnade's columns (facing the [land side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_side "Land side")) are 65 feet (20 m) high, while the southern colonnade's columns (facing the [air side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_side "Air side")) are 40 feet (12 m) high.[\[e\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-58) The columns are all made of [reinforced concrete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforced_concrete "Reinforced concrete"),[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Merkel_p._223-59)[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-AF-1961-09-60) which is [bush hammered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bush_hammer "Bush hammer");[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-AF_p._82-21) the [rebar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebar "Rebar"), or reinforcing steel, in the columns was manufactured by [Bethlehem Steel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bethlehem_Steel "Bethlehem Steel").[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-61) Each of the taller columns has 20 short tons (18 long tons; 18 t) of reinforcing steel, while each of the shorter columns is reinforced by 16 short tons (14 long tons; 15 t) of steel.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Merkel_p._223-59) The columns slant outward at an angle of either 10[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Hailey_1960-7) or 15 degrees,[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Forgey_p241-62) counteracting the forces of suspension cables that carry the roof.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Hailey_1960-7)[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Ashton_1961-43) At the top of each column are edge beams, which hold the roof's cables in place.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-AR_p._178-63)[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Ichniowski_1996-64) When the terminal was extended west and east in the 1990s, the new columns were built to the same dimensions as the original terminals' columns.[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Forgey_p241-62)[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Ichniowski_1996-64)

The landside columns support a canopy that protrudes 43 feet (13 m) above the landside drop-off ramp.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Hailey_1960-7)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Armstrong_1960-14) The [curtain walls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curtain_wall_/(architecture/) "Curtain wall (architecture)") between the columns are made of glass,[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Ashton_1961-43)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Stroud_p._558-8) slanting outward at the same angle as the columns.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Wells_1962-65) Each glass pane is placed on rubber [gaskets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gasket "Gasket") and fastened to the columns using rubber strips;[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Grant_1962-66) these gaskets tended to fall off after they were installed.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Freeman_p._66-67) The [Pittsburgh Plate Glass Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Plate_Glass "Pittsburgh Plate Glass") made 70,000 square feet (6,500 m2) of glass for the terminal, which were cut into 1,137 shapes.[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-68) The window panes are embedded within aluminum frames, which are curved and tilt outward at their tops.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-AF_p._77-69) The curtain walls in the annexes are similar in style to the original curtain walls, though they use modern gaskets that were less susceptible to falling.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Freeman_p._66-67)

The roof is composed of [precast concrete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Precast_concrete "Precast concrete") panels,[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-AF_p._82-21)[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-AR_p._178-63) suspended between cables that span the width of the building.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Giles_1960-42)[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Public_Opinion_1961-70) Nitterhouse Concrete Products in Pennsylvania manufactured the slabs.[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Public_Opinion_1961-70) There are 1,792 concrete slabs in the roof, which each weigh 800 pounds (360 kg) and measure 7.5 inches (190 mm) thick, including a 1.5-inch-thick (38 mm) styrofoam layer on the underside of each panel. The slabs, which measure 8+2⁄3 by 5+11⁄12 feet (2.6 by 1.8 m) across, create a deck spanning 89,800 square feet (8,340 m2).[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Public_Opinion_1961-70) The cables, similar in design to the suspenders used on [suspension bridges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suspension_bridge "Suspension bridge"), are 1 inch (25 mm) in diameter[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-AR_p._178-63)[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Public_Opinion_1961-70) and are spaced 10 feet (3.0 m) apart.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Armstrong_1960-14)[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-AR_p._178-63) Concrete stiffening ribs encase each of the cables,[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-AF_p._77-69)[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Merkel_pp._222%E2%80%93223-71) preventing the cables from bouncing around;[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-AR_p._178-63) these ribs are 14 to 16 inches (360 to 410 mm) deep.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Ichniowski_1996-64) Because the columns are slanted outward, the ribs are about 160 feet (49 m) or 170 feet (52 m) wide.[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-AF_p._80-72)

To improve acoustics, the roof dips at the centerline of the terminal,[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Armstrong_1960-14)[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Jones_1962-32)[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Ashton_1961-43) reaching as low as 26 feet (7.9 m)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Hailey_1960-7) or 28 feet (8.5 m).[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Friedlander_1962-57) The roof's centerline slopes down from both ends toward a drainpipe at the center of the building.[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Sehlstedt_1962-73)[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-AF_p._80-72) The drainpipe is about 30 inches (760 mm) wide[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Sehlstedt_1962-73) and can drain 12,500 US gallons (47 m3) from the roof every minute.[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-AF_p._80-72) Water from the drainpipe is funneled into a [catch basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catch_basin "Catch basin") nearby.[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-74) The roofs over the 1990s extensions are similar in design to the original roof.[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Forgey_p241-62)

Originally, the terminal spanned 500,000 square feet (46,000 m2).[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-World_Airport_Week_1997-75)[\[f\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-76) During a 1996 expansion, the size of the Main Terminal was more than doubled,[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Reid_1996-41)[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Potomac_News_1996-77) increasing to about 1.1 million square feet (100,000 m2).[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-flydulles.com_1962-9)[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Potomac_News_1996-77) The interiors were initially designed in a palette of green, blue, brown, and gray hues, to match the landscape.[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Gustaitis_1962-78) Originally, the Main Terminal's upper level was for departing passengers, while the lower level was for arriving passengers.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Mehaffy_p._4.8-46) The west and east wings have a combined 600,000 square feet (56,000 m2) and contain an additional basement level that is not present under the original terminal.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Ichniowski_1996-64)

#### Structural and mechanical features

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Structural and mechanical features")\]

The cable roof allowed Saarinen to construct the upper story without columns.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Armstrong_1960-14)[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Jones_1962-32) The lower story sits on a concrete floor slab, and the upper story's floor slab is made of reinforced concrete. On the lower story, columns are placed at regular intervals, supporting concrete beams above; these beams are aligned with the colonnades on the facade. The lower-story columns flare outward at their bases purely for decorative purposes.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-AR_p._178-63) The original interiors are divided into [bays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_/(architecture/) "Bay (architecture)") measuring 40 by 150 feet (12 by 46 m), spanning the terminal's entire width and corresponding to the facade's bays. Each interior bay could be configured with its own ticket counter, baggage facility, concessions, and two loading bays for mobile lounges. Saarinen's original design allowed 40 feet (12 m) bays to be added on either end of the terminal as necessary.[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-79)

Saarinen's master plan for Dulles Airport called for service buildings both east and west of the Main Terminal; these structures were designed with low roofs so they did not obstruct views from the Main Terminal. The original service building, to the east, included equipment for hot and chilled water production.[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-80) When the terminal was completed, it was cooled by two large refrigeration units, which had a daily cooling capacity equivalent to 2 million pounds (900 t) of ice.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-81)

[![Image 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b5/2022-03-24_13_43_30_UTC_minus_4_Ticketing_and_check-in_section_within_the_main_terminal_at_Washington_Dulles_International_Airport_in_the_Dulles_section_of_Sterling%2C_Loudoun_County%2C_Virginia.jpg/250px-thumbnail.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2022-03-24_13_43_30_UTC_minus_4_Ticketing_and_check-in_section_within_the_main_terminal_at_Washington_Dulles_International_Airport_in_the_Dulles_section_of_Sterling,_Loudoun_County,_Virginia.jpg)

Interior of the upper level, with ticket counters at left and the curtain wall at right (2022)

When the terminal was built, there were ticket counters on the upper level, and conveyor belts that brought baggage to a loading area in the basement.[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Bradley_1962-82) The ticket counters were originally grouped into three clusters.[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Sehlstedt_1962-73) In addition, there were various stores, three seating areas with aluminum and vinyl benches, along with two large departure screens.[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Bradley_1962-82) The original design included very few stores,[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-83) since it was not originally envisioned as a place to spend extended amounts of time.[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-84) When the terminal opened, there were 24 mobile-lounge gates.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Kohlmeier_1962-28)[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Friedlander_1962-57)[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Riley_1963-85) Many of the mobile-lounge gates were subsequently closed with the implementation of stringent security procedures, and some of these gates were infilled with glass in the 1990s.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Freeman_p._67-36) When the terminal was expanded west and east in the 1990s, stores and ticket counters were built in both wings;[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Reingold_1994-38)[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Reid_1996-41) the annexes have similar terrazzo floors and concrete surfaces to the original terminal.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Freeman_p._67-36) Until the 2000s, the upper story also had security-screening areas.[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-USA_Today_j755-86)

The lower, or ground, story initially contained regional and commuter airline gates, along with offices[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Rife_1968-53) and baggage carousels.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Mehaffy_p._4.8-46)[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Cowan_1990a-87) The lower level also includes a "Dulles Diamond" security screening facility for frequent travelers,[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Yu_2009-88)[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_Washington_Post_2009-89) as well as baggage carousels and a baggage-sorting facility in the west wing.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Reid_1996-41) Escalators connect the upper and lower levels, allowing arriving passengers to pick up their baggage.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Armstrong_1960-14)[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Giles_1960-42) The south concourse had marble tables and upholstered seats.[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Bradley_1962-82) There was also a reflecting pool in the south concourse, along with lounges on a balcony level overlooking the concourse.[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Gustaitis_1962-78) Basements under both wings accommodate baggage handling facilities,[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Freeman_p._67-36)[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Ichniowski_1996-64) and there are two basements beneath the original terminal.[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-USA_Today_j755-86)[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Weiss_2008-90) The original structure's first or upper basement contains security checkpoints spanning 121,700 square feet (11,310 m2);[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Yu_2009-88)[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-91) the 8,500-square-foot (790 m2) Capital One Lounge is located between the western and eastern checkpoints.[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Clabaugh_2023-92) The second or lower basement contains a 54,500-square-foot (5,060 m2) station for the [AeroTrain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AeroTrain_/(Dulles_International_Airport/) "AeroTrain (Dulles International Airport)") people-mover system.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Weiss_2008-90)

The taxi and bus–limousine drop-off areas lead directly to the terminal's upper level, and a ramp and escalators lead from the private automobile drop-off areas to the upper level.[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Bradley_1962-82) A 1,000-foot-long (300 m) underpass with [moving walkways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moving_walkway "Moving walkway") links the Main Terminal to parking garages and the Dulles International Airport station.[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Cline_2022-93) The underpass is accessed from the terminal via elevators[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Cline_2022-93) and a pair of escalators.[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-94) Another 1,000-foot-long (300 m) tunnel leads south from the Main Terminal to midfield concourse B.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-flydulles.com_1962-9) Escalators and elevators also descend to the basements.[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-95)

[![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/82/Dulles_International_Airport_mobile_lounges_00769v_%281%29.jpg/250px-Dulles_International_Airport_mobile_lounges_00769v_%281%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dulles_International_Airport_mobile_lounges_00769v_/(1/).jpg)

The terminal with its original mobile lounges (c. 1962)

Initially, after passengers were processed at the Main Terminal, they were transported directly to planes via mobile lounges.[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-PA6_p._304-96)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Schwartz_p._50-15) The original mobile lounges were manufactured by [Budd Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Budd_Company "Budd Company") and [Chrysler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chrysler "Chrysler").[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Hailey_1961-97)[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Roth_2025-98) They were similar to [airside transfer buses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airport_bus#Airside_transfer "Airport bus"), except that the lounges were intended as movable extensions of the terminal itself,[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Mehaffy_p._4.8-46)[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-AR_p._180-99) with floors at the same height as the departure level.[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-PA6_p._304-96)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Schwartz_p._50-15) Each lounge had doorways and adjustable ramps at both ends,[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-AF_p._82-21)[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-AR_p._180-99) along with seats similar to those in the Main Terminal.[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Bradley_1962-82) Though the floor could be raised and lowered to accommodate different plane models' heights,[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-PA6_p._304-96)[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-AR_p._180-99) it could not rise above 13 feet (4.0 m).[\[94\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_New_York_Times_1969-100) Each mobile lounge could travel at a top speed of about 25 mph (40 km/h).[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Friedlander_1962-57)[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Riley_1963-85) Departure times originally reflected when the lounges left the terminal,[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Kohlmeier_1962-28)[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Friedlander_1962-57) and larger planes were served by multiple lounges.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Friedlander_1962-57) The Plane Mate, a variant of the mobile lounge, was introduced in the early 1970s[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Vanderbilt_j360-101)[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Roth_2025-98) to accommodate [wide-body aircraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wide-body_aircraft "Wide-body aircraft").[\[96\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Pillsbury_1978-102) In contrast to the lower capacity of the original lounges,[\[g\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-104) the Plane Mates could fit 150 passengers and could rise higher than the original lounges.[\[94\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_New_York_Times_1969-100)[\[98\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-105)

Saarinen considered the mobile lounges a solution to three problems—they shortened the walking distance to the plane, reduced [taxiing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxiing "Taxiing") distances, and allowed greater [apron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airport_apron "Airport apron") flexibility.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Sehlstedt_1962a-29)[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Merkel_p._216-20)[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Roman_p._116-22) When the terminal was developed in the 1960s, jet planes could not fit traditional terminals and could only be accessed via long [jetways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jetway "Jetway").[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Vanderbilt_j360-101) The mobile lounges eliminated the need for jetways[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Merkel_p._216-20)[\[99\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_New_York_Times_1962-106) and allowed Dulles Airport to be built with a single terminal, smaller in size than other airports' terminals.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-McLeod_1959-12) They were also intended to increase operational flexibility, because planes no longer had to unload passengers next to the terminal,[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Merkel_p._216-20)[\[100\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Stepp_1959-107) while also reducing airlines' taxiing fees and keeping aircraft emissions away from the terminal.[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Bennett_1964-108) Passengers also did not have to walk more than a few hundred feet.[\[h\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-110)

Retrospectively, observers noted that the lounges were inconvenient to use[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-111) and that passengers making [connecting flights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connecting_flight "Connecting flight") had to wait for multiple lounges.[\[104\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Gottdiener_2001-112) When the midfield concourses were built in the 1980s, the mobile lounges began traveling to these concourses instead.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Schwartz_p._50-15)[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Field_1999-16) The [AeroTrain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AeroTrain_/(Dulles_International_Airport/) "AeroTrain (Dulles International Airport)") people mover system opened in 2010, traveling to midfield concourses A, B, and C.[\[105\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-113) As of 2025, Dulles Airport's operator [Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Washington_Airports_Authority "Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority") retains 19 of Saarinen's mobile lounges and 30 Plane Mates, which operate to Concourse D.[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-McCaffrey_v490-103)[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Roth_2025-98) There are also plans to extend the AeroTrain to Concourse E, a future midfield concourse;[\[106\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-114)[\[107\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Montgomery_h123-115) the potential expansion of the AeroTrain would make the remaining mobile lounges obsolete.[\[107\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Montgomery_h123-115)

The [U.S. Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_United_States_Congress "81st United States Congress") passed the Washington Inner Airports Act in 1950 to provide funding for a new airport in the [Washington metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_metropolitan_area "Washington metropolitan area").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Mehaffy_p._S4-1)[\[108\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-116) This directly led to the creation of what became [Dulles International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport "Dulles International Airport") in [Chantilly, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chantilly,_Virginia "Chantilly, Virginia").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Mehaffy_p._S4-1) President [Dwight Eisenhower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dwight_Eisenhower "Dwight Eisenhower") selected the 8,000-acre (3,200 ha) Chantilly site in January 1958,[\[109\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-117) and the U.S. government acquired the land that August.[\[110\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-118) The airport was officially named in 1959 after [John Foster Dulles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Foster_Dulles "John Foster Dulles"), the [United States Secretary of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_State "United States Secretary of State") under Eisenhower.[\[111\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-119) The airport and its Main Terminal were originally controlled directly by the U.S. federal government[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-World_Airport_Week_1997-75) through the [Federal Aviation Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Aviation_Administration "Federal Aviation Administration") (FAA).[\[112\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-120)

[![Image 7](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/af/2022-03-24_13_47_19_UTC_minus_4_Ticketing_and_check-in_section_within_the_main_terminal_at_Washington_Dulles_International_Airport_in_the_Dulles_section_of_Sterling%2C_Loudoun_County%2C_Virginia.jpg/250px-thumbnail.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2022-03-24_13_47_19_UTC_minus_4_Ticketing_and_check-in_section_within_the_main_terminal_at_Washington_Dulles_International_Airport_in_the_Dulles_section_of_Sterling,_Loudoun_County,_Virginia.jpg)

Interior (2022)

The [Civil Aeronautics Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_Aeronautics_Administration_/(United_States/) "Civil Aeronautics Administration (United States)") (CAA) selected [Eero Saarinen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eero_Saarinen "Eero Saarinen") of [Bloomfield Hills, Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloomfield_Hills,_Michigan "Bloomfield Hills, Michigan"), in May 1958 to design several of Dulles Airport's buildings, including its Main Terminal and control tower.[\[113\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_Washington_Post_and_Times_Herald_1958a-121)[\[114\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-122) [Ammann & Whitney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ammann_%26_Whitney "Ammann & Whitney"), who led the airport's overall design,[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Merkel_p._216-20)[\[113\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_Washington_Post_and_Times_Herald_1958a-121) had previously worked with Saarinen on [Ellinikon International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellinikon_International_Airport "Ellinikon International Airport")'s terminal.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Merkel_p._216-20) At the time, Saarinen was busy designing the [TWA Flight Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TWA_Flight_Center "TWA Flight Center") at [Idlewild Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idlewild_Airport "Idlewild Airport") in New York.[\[115\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Roman_p._111-123) Saarinen and Ammann & Whitney worked in collaboration with the airport's mechanical engineering firm [Burns & McDonnell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burns_%26_McDonnell "Burns & McDonnell") and the consultant Charles Landrum to collect data for the design of Dulles Airport's Main Terminal.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Merkel_p._216-20)[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Roman_p._116-22) They studied airport operations, including the distances passengers had to walk to access planes, at airports across the U.S.;[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Merkel_p._216-20)[\[115\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Roman_p._111-123) the team found that, on average, passengers had to walk 900 feet (270 m) from terminal to plane.[\[116\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-124) The design team was particularly focused on reducing passengers' walking distances, reducing [taxiing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxiing "Taxiing") costs, and increasing flexibility of the apron.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Roman_p._116-22)[\[117\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-AR_p._179-125) Furthermore, they anticipated that Dulles Airport would need 60 [gates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gate_/(airport/) "Gate (airport)") by 1975 to accommodate increasing demand.[\[117\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-AR_p._179-125)

Saarinen sketched his initial designs on [legal paper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legal_paper "Legal paper").[\[118\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-126) One early design proposal, by Boyd Anderson of Ammann & Whitney, called for suspension cables between the ground and roof; after Saarinen expressed his satisfaction, the design team instead proposed a cable roof.[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Forgey_p241-62) The CAA reviewed Saarinen's preliminary ideas for the terminal in October 1958.[\[119\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_Washington_Post_and_Times_Herald_1958-127) A key component of the plan was mobile lounges that would travel from the terminal directly to planes, eliminating many of the inflexibilities of jetways and fixed gates.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Merkel_p._216-20)[\[119\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_Washington_Post_and_Times_Herald_1958-127) The terminal itself was tentatively planned to have separate levels for departing and arriving passengers.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-McLeod_1959-12)[\[120\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-128) Contracts for clearing and grading the site had been awarded by the end of 1958, but no contracts for the terminal had been awarded yet.[\[121\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-129) The terminal design was still in progress by early 1959, at which point it was planned to span 300,000 square feet (28,000 m2).[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-McLeod_1959-12)[\[100\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Stepp_1959-107) Although no details had been announced at the time, the [_Evening Star_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evening_Star_/(Washington_D.C./) "Evening Star (Washington D.C.)") described the design as "something revolutionary".[\[100\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Stepp_1959-107)

Saarinen's friend [Charles Eames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Eames "Charles Eames") prepared a short film about the mobile lounges to convince airport officials of their efficacy.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Roman_p._116-22)[\[122\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-130) The FAA (then known as the [Federal Aviation Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Aviation_Agency "Federal Aviation Agency")) announced details of Saarinen's design in January 1960.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Hailey_1960-7)[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_New_York_Times_1960-109) The plans called for a 600-by-150-foot (183 by 46 m) double-level structure, with concrete piers supporting a concave curved roof; the building could be doubled in size.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Hailey_1960-7)[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_Times_1960-24) To reduce confusion, departing and arriving passengers were segregated on different levels.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Giles_1960-42) Saarinen and his associates wanted the design to symbolize the [Jet Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jet_Age "Jet Age") while also complementing the classical [architecture of Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Architecture_of_Washington,_D.C. "Architecture of Washington, D.C.")[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Ashton_1961-43)[\[123\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-131) The [control tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Control_tower "Control tower") and mobile lounges were designed in conjunction with the terminal;[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Hailey_1960-7)[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_Times_1960-24) the lounges in particular made it possible to reduce the building's size, since long passageways were no longer needed.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-McLeod_1959-12)[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Sehlstedt_1962a-29) The final design, including mobile lounges, was selected after the FAA examined over 100 proposals.[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Hailey_1961-97)

The FAA awarded contracts for the terminal's heating and cooling systems in August 1959.[\[124\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-132) That October, it ordered a prototype of a mobile lounge[\[125\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-133) and awarded a contract for the terminal's telephone service.[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-134) The FAA also built [settling basins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Settling_basin "Settling basin") for temporary use until a permanent sewage system for the terminal could be built.[\[127\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-135) The FAA began soliciting bids for the terminal building itself in January 1960[\[128\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-136) and reviewed the bids the next month.[\[129\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-137) The Corbetta Construction Company of New York City submitted the lowest bid, for $4,432,000,[\[130\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-138)[\[131\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-139) and was subsequently awarded the construction contract.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Hailey_1960a-23) That April, workers began grading the terminal's site and laying [foundations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foundation_/(engineering/) "Foundation (engineering)").[\[132\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-140) Models of the Main Terminal were displayed at [Washington National Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_National_Airport "Washington National Airport") in August 1960.[\[133\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Kornberg_1960-141) By then, the U.S. federal government (which originally operated the airport) had [oversubscribed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overselling "Overselling") all of the ticket counter space and the gates.[\[134\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_New_York_Times_1960a-142)[\[133\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Kornberg_1960-141) The demand for ticket counter space was already one-third higher than what was available.[\[134\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_New_York_Times_1960a-142)

[![Image 8](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/99/Dulles_International_Airport_%281970%29.jpg/250px-Dulles_International_Airport_%281970%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dulles_International_Airport_/(1970/).jpg)

The original terminal seen from the northeast (1970)

The Main Terminal's structural work was half complete by October 1960. At that point, concrete for the lower level had been poured, and workers had erected steel framework on the north and south side of the building, in preparation for the construction of the columns.[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Hailey_1960b-56) By the end of the year, the airport was unlikely to be completed by its originally-projected opening date of July 1961,[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Hailey_1960a-23)[\[135\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-143) so outgoing FAA administrator [Pete Quesada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Quesada "Pete Quesada") postponed the opening date by one year.[\[136\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-144) By June 1961, the airport's original $85 million budget had more than doubled to $175 million, and FAA administrator [Najeeb Halaby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Najeeb_Halaby "Najeeb Halaby") said the new terminal would be overcrowded by 1967.[\[137\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-145) Due to a lack of federal funding, the building's initial length was truncated from 1,200 to 600 feet (370 to 180 m).[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Ichniowski_1996-64)

The terminal was still under construction when Saarinen suddenly died in September 1961,[\[138\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-146) at which point it was budgeted at $12 million.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Ashton_1961-43) For the construction of each column, workers poured concrete around multiple tons of steel [rebar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebar "Rebar").[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Merkel_p._223-59)[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-AF-1961-09-60) The rebar in each column surrounded a metal cage, from which a worker oversaw the pour until it was nearly complete; the cage was then encased in concrete.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Merkel_p._223-59) Workers pre-stressed the roof's cables by loading sandbags onto them, thus allowing the cables to carry the roof panels without sagging significantly.[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Forgey_p241-62) The cables were strung between each pair of columns, then bent into shape using concrete blocks and encased in concrete;[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Merkel_p._223-59) their installation required many complex computations.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-AF-1961-09-60) The concrete roof ribs were test-loaded after being poured.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-AF-1961-09-60)[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Merkel_pp._222%E2%80%93223-71) No stationary [scaffolding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scaffolding "Scaffolding") was used for the terminal's construction, though the roof was built using a movable scaffold.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Merkel_p._223-59)[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-AF_p._77-69)

Thirteen airlines had leased space at the airport by late 1961.[\[139\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-New_York_Herald_Tribune_1961-147) That November, the FAA awarded a concession for the terminal's bars and restaurants.[\[140\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-148) The FAA paid $4.6 million for the terminal's first 20 mobile lounges that month,[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Hailey_1961-97) but the airlines hesitated at paying the cost.[\[139\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-New_York_Herald_Tribune_1961-147) The airlines were also reluctant to give the FAA specifications for space at the terminal until they knew how much their leases would cost. As such, that December, Halaby threatened to take over the design of each airline's spaces unless the airlines provided specifications within two weeks.[\[141\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-149) By then, the control tower was 60% complete.[\[142\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-150) The airlines agreed to lease the Main Terminal's 456-foot (139 m) ticket counter in January 1962, having petitioned for a longer counter.[\[143\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-151) Disputes over fees continued until that June, when the FAA and the airlines agreed on a schedule of operating fees for the mobile lounges and the terminal's space.[\[144\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-152)

The terminal's contractors began working double shifts in April 1962 after Halaby threatened to penalize contractors for not completing the terminal by October 1.[\[145\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-153) During mid-1962, the FAA solicited bids for the construction of service spaces for the airlines.[\[146\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-154) Builders had difficulties constructing the windows;[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Wells_1962-65)[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Grant_1962-66) as late as June 1962, none of the glass had been installed.[\[147\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-155) Workers eventually built a custom protractor to cut the glass.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Wells_1962-65)[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Grant_1962-66) Because the windows were to slope outward, workers fitted gaskets around each window to prevent them from tipping over.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Grant_1962-66) The FAA announced in August 1962 that the terminal and the rest of the airport would be dedicated that November.[\[99\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_New_York_Times_1962-106)[\[148\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-156) By then, workers were finishing the interior, while airport staff were practicing with the mobile lounges.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Grant_1962-66) Numerous shops had been leased out,[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Grant_1962-66) and additional retailers leased space at the terminal that October.[\[149\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-157) As late as a few days before the opening, many parts of the terminal were still incomplete.[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Bradley_1962-82)[\[150\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-158) The final cost was estimated at approximately $16 million.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-AF_p._82-21)[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Rife_1968-53)

### Opening and early use

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Opening and early use")\]

[![Image 9](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/34/Dulles_Airport_terminal_windows.jpg/250px-Dulles_Airport_terminal_windows.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dulles_Airport_terminal_windows.jpg)

The western end of the terminal, facing the landside facade (2025)

On November 17, 1962, former president Eisenhower and U.S. President [John F. Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy "John F. Kennedy") dedicated the airport with a ceremony at the terminal, attended by an estimated 60,000 people.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Boston_Globe_1962-3)[\[151\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Munsey_1962-159) The first passengers began using the terminal two days later,[\[152\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-160) and the terminal recorded 25,000 tourists on its first full Sunday of operation.[\[153\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-161) Some final work was still ongoing,[\[151\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Munsey_1962-159) with 15% of the work still incomplete at the time of opening.[\[154\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Howard_k402-162) The terminal quickly became a symbol of the new airport,[\[155\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Baker_1962-163) and it received positive acclaim, in part because its mobile lounges made the planes entirely [accessible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accessibility "Accessibility").[\[156\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Haugland_m168-164) Travelers often threw coins into the terminal's reflecting
