pool;[\[154\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Howard_k402-162)[\[156\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Haugland_m168-164) the proceeds were donated to charity.[\[157\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Newsweek_1965-165) The FAA leased out a [duty-free shop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duty-free_shop "Duty-free shop") at the terminal in early 1963,[\[158\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-166) and a restaurant opened there that November, at which point the terminal was basically complete.[\[154\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Howard_k402-162)

Dulles was initially considered a [white elephant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_elephant "White elephant"), being far from Washington, D.C., with few flights;[\[96\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Pillsbury_1978-102)[\[159\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Davis_1966-167) this had a negative effect on the terminal concessionaires' business.[\[160\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_New_York_Times_1964-168) _[Newsweek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newsweek "Newsweek")_ said that staff sometimes outnumbered passengers,[\[157\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Newsweek_1965-165) and _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")_ wrote that "the terminal has entertained nearly twice as many viewers as travelers".[\[161\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Loftus_z664-169) Another source said that "once a visitor could roll a bowling ball from one end ... without hitting anyone".[\[162\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-170) Conversely, the terminal was popular as a tourist attraction,[\[157\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Newsweek_1965-165)_[\[161\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Loftus_z664-169)[\[163\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-McDowell_p888-171)_ and the mobile lounges had become more popular than expected;[\[161\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Loftus_z664-169)[\[164\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-172) many visitors paid just to ride the lounges.[\[165\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_New_York_Times_1973-173) The terminal and airport continued to experience lower-than-expected patronage in the mid-1960s.[\[157\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Newsweek_1965-165)[\[160\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_New_York_Times_1964-168) Two of the terminal's concessionaires had gone out of business by 1966, while other concessionaires paid discounted rents.[\[166\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Schorr_1966-174) At that point, there were somewhat less than a million annual passengers,[\[159\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Davis_1966-167) and only half the mobile lounges were needed.[\[166\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Schorr_1966-174) In 1968, the lower level flooded, causing some damage to the terminal.[\[167\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-175) Patronage steadily increased; by 1969, some concessionaires had recorded their first profits.[\[168\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-176)

### 1970s and early 1980s

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: 1970s and early 1980s")\]

By the early 1970s, the FAA anticipated that the terminal's usage would increase sixfold, from 2 to 12 million, within a decade.[\[169\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-177)[\[170\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Donnelly_1972-178) To accommodate the increased traffic, the FAA ordered additional mobile lounges and stopped giving tourists rides on the existing lounges,[\[165\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_New_York_Times_1973-173) and U.S. President [Richard Nixon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Nixon "Richard Nixon") allocated $7 million for a possible expansion of the Main Terminal.[\[171\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Ashworth_1970-179) Early plans called for the building to be lengthened east–west to 920 feet (280 m), increasing hourly capacity from 1,650 to either 2,300[\[171\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Ashworth_1970-179) or 2,500 passengers.[\[172\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-St._Louis_Post-Dispatch_1970-180) The architectural firm [Hellmuth, Obata & Kassabaum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HOK_/(firm/) "HOK (firm)") (HOK) was hired in December 1970 to prepare preliminary designs for the expansion.[\[172\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-St._Louis_Post-Dispatch_1970-180) When the [National Capital Planning Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Capital_Planning_Commission "National Capital Planning Commission") (NCPC) approved the plans in 1972,[\[173\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Hodge_1977-181) the project was estimated to cost $12 million.[\[170\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Donnelly_1972-178) HOK and [Peat, Marwick & Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peat,_Marwick,_Mitchell "Peat, Marwick, Mitchell") were hired to develop an expansion plan for the terminal, but no progress occurred for several years,[\[174\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Huxtable_o904-182)[\[175\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Ashworth_1976-183) in part because of funding shortages and insufficient demand.[\[173\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Hodge_1977-181)

[![Image 10](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ca/Dulles_Terminal_-_3.jpg/250px-Dulles_Terminal_-_3.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dulles_Terminal_-_3.jpg)

The landside facade (2023)

The expansion plans were renewed in 1976, when the FAA directed Peat, Marwick & Mitchell to revise the airport's master plan.[\[175\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Ashworth_1976-183) At that point, the terminal expansion was planned to cost $15 million;[\[175\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Ashworth_1976-183) it was to be part of a $150–190 million overhaul of the airport.[\[176\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Morris_1977-184) The NCPC expressed concerns that the east–west annexes would overshadow the original design,[\[173\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Hodge_1977-181) and preservationists advocated for the terminal to be designated as a landmark, restricting changes to the structure.[\[174\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Huxtable_o904-182) Ultimately, HOK designed two small annexes along the southern facade for additional mobile lounge gates.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-A-1988-05-26) These annexes measured 50 feet (15 m) wide,[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-A-1988-05-26)[\[177\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Morris_1978-185) about the same as the mobile lounges' lengths, and were built in a similar style to the original terminal.[\[178\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-186) The FAA hired Frank Briscoe Co. in early 1978 to expand the terminal,[\[179\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-187) and work began that September.[\[177\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Morris_1978-185) The same year, the control tower's radome was replaced.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Kelly_j193-54) The project freed up space in the original terminal for baggage handling,[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-A-1988-05-26)[\[177\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Morris_1978-185) and the FAA awarded a contract to expand the baggage-handling facilities in late 1979.[\[180\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-188) HOK's expansion was completed in 1980.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Freeman_p._67-36)[\[181\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-AJ-1980-11-189) By then, customs facilities had been moved to an adjacent temporary structure with four mobile-lounge bays.[\[181\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-AJ-1980-11-189)

The expansion came just as patronage at Dulles Airport dropped sharply, in part because of the inconvenience of accessing and using the airport.[\[182\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-190)[\[183\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Battle_Creek_Enquirer_c578-191) To attract business, the FAA began allowing small planes to load or unload directly at the terminal itself.[\[183\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Battle_Creek_Enquirer_c578-191) The FAA rejected plans to add more airline gates to the terminal, citing esthetic concerns and a lack of space.[\[184\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-192) Instead, in 1983, the agency proposed a "midfield concourse" in the middle of the apron, from which passengers could load onto planes directly.[\[185\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-193) The first midfield concourse was hastily built and could be accessed only by the mobile lounges.[\[186\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-194)

### Master plan expansion

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Master plan expansion")\]

#### Mid- and late 1980s

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Mid- and late 1980s")\]

In the mid-1980s, as part of a master plan, a consultant recommended doubling the Main Terminal's size, constructing a people-mover to the midfield concourse, and expanding the terminal's airline gates.[\[187\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-195) New vehicular ramps were proposed to alleviate traffic in front of the terminal.[\[188\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Henderson_1987a-196) The plans also included new facilities for several airlines that used the Main Terminal,[\[189\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_New_York_Times_1985-197)[\[190\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_Business_Review_1986-198) along with a separate terminal for international arrivals.[\[188\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Henderson_1987a-196)[\[191\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Cowan_1990-199) The expansions came amid rapid growth in the airport's usage, which neared 4 million by 1984.[\[192\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-200)[\[189\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_New_York_Times_1985-197) The master plan was approved by the NCPC in 1986,[\[193\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-201) at which point was expected to cost $420 million.[\[194\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-202)[\[195\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Henderson_1987-203) In the meantime, a clinic, baggage claim areas, and stores in the terminal were added, while the international arrivals area was revamped.[\[190\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_Business_Review_1986-198)

The [Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Washington_Airports_Authority "Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority") (MWAA) took over Dulles Airport's operation in 1987 and assumed responsibility for the expansion program.[\[195\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Henderson_1987-203)[\[196\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-204) [David Childs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Childs "David Childs") and Marilyn Taylor of [Skidmore, Owings & Merrill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skidmore,_Owings_%26_Merrill "Skidmore, Owings & Merrill") (SOM) were hired to design a master plan for the terminal, which was rapidly approaching its annual capacity of 13 million passengers.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-A-1988-05-26) Passengers in the terminal frequently had to wait hours to get their luggage, and the [departure boards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departure_board "Departure board") could not display all the flights.[\[197\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_Daily_Progress_1989-205) Concessions and security equipment had been installed throughout the years, intruding on the original interior design.[\[198\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-206) Security concerns had also required the mobile-lounge docks on the south facade to be closed; instead, passengers had to undergo X-ray screening, creating a [bottleneck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bottleneck_/(production/) "Bottleneck (production)").[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Freeman_p._67-36)

The MWAA banned smoking inside the terminal in 1988.[\[199\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-207) The same year, to alleviate congestion at the Main Terminal, the MWAA began constructing the international arrivals terminal,[\[200\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-208) which was designed by SOM to the west of the original terminal.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Freeman_p._63-31) The MWAA also developed a satellite facility with a baggage check and duty-free shop in [Downtown Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_/(Washington,_D.C./) "Downtown (Washington, D.C.)"), which opened in 1989, further relieving crowding.[\[201\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-209) At that point, the Main Terminal's expansion was scheduled to be completed by early 1994.[\[197\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_Daily_Progress_1989-205) In the meantime, the MWAA added temporary gates to the terminal, which consisted of [semi-trailers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semi-trailer "Semi-trailer"); since these trailers were intended as temporary structures, they did not need to undergo a historic-preservation review.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Reingold_1994-38)

A baggage-claim area was added inside the terminal in 1990,[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Cowan_1990a-87) and a federal inspection area at the Main Terminal was enlarged as well.[\[202\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-210) The International Arrivals Terminal opened in 1991, replacing the international-arrivals facilities in the Main Terminal,[\[203\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-211) though the new terminal quickly became overcrowded.[\[204\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-212) The MWAA was also constructing permanent midfield concourses,[\[205\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-213) replacing the temporary annexes on the main building's southern facade.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-A-1988-05-26) The Main Terminal's annexes were tentatively scheduled to be completed in 1993;[\[191\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Cowan_1990-199) the extensions would incorporate a similar curved roof to the original terminal, which would remain visible from the Dulles Access Road.[\[206\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-214) Despite calls by [United Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Airlines "United Airlines") officials to halt or delay the proposed expansion,[\[207\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-215) the MWAA decided to proceed with the renovation, the cost of which had risen to $319 million.[\[208\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-216) The control tower's radome was replaced again in 1993.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Kelly_j193-54)

By 1993, workers had upgraded the airport's utilities to support the terminal's expansion, which was scheduled to be completed in 1996[\[209\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Fehr_1993-217) or 1997.[\[210\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Moore_1992-218) This was planned to be followed in 1998 by the original terminal's interior.[\[209\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Fehr_1993-217) By that time, Dulles had over 11 million annual passengers,[\[209\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Fehr_1993-217)[\[210\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Moore_1992-218)[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Arch_p._40-30) and airport officials were considering replacing the once-novel mobile lounges with a people mover.[\[211\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-219) Work on the expansion began in October 1993,[\[212\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-220) though MWAA officials were already contemplating further upgrades before work started.[\[213\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-221) To fund the renovation, the MWAA added a [passenger facility charge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passenger_facility_charge "Passenger facility charge") to every ticket,[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Reingold_1994-38) and it issued [bonds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bond_/(finance/) "Bond (finance)") to cover seven-tenths of the cost.[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Potomac_News_1996-77)[\[214\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Danville_Register_and_Bee_1996-222) The Main Terminal was lengthened to 1,240 feet (380 m), slightly more than twice the original length,[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Cullerton_1996-39)[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Reid_1996-41) and the vehicular ramps were also expanded.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Cullerton_1996-39)[\[215\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-223) The columns and roofs of the original building were recreated in the annexes,[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Forgey_p241-62)[\[216\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-224) though the annexes' roof cables were prestressed using cranes rather than sandbags.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Ichniowski_1996-64) The framework for the eastern extension was finished by late 1995, with the western extension still underway.[\[217\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-225)

[United Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Airlines "United Airlines") moved into the eastern annex on July 1, 1996,[\[218\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-226) and the annexes were dedicated on September 6 that year.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Reid_1996-41)[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Potomac_News_1996-77) Afterward, the MWAA announced plans to renovate the original terminal's ceiling, which required [asbestos abatement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asbestos_abatement "Asbestos abatement").[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Freeman_p._67-36)[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Reid_1996-41) The MWAA was also relocating the concessions to provide more space for queuing,[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Freeman_p._67-36) and it finished replacing the vehicular ramps outside the terminal in 1997.[\[219\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-227) Additional midfield concourses opened in the late 1990s, relieving crowding at the Main Terminal, where queues had frequently doubled back on themselves.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Field_1999-16) At the time, there were proposals for an underground walkway (and, later, a people mover) leading to the midfield concourses.[\[220\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-228) Development of the walkway was delayed after U.S. Senator [John McCain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McCain "John McCain") withheld congressional funds for the project, stemming from a dispute regarding flights at Washington National Airport.[\[221\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-229)

[![Image 11: The AeroTrain station in the Main Terminal's second basement](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/50/2015-09-29_23_37_05_AeroTrain_station_at_the_main_terminal_of_Washington_Dulles_International_Airport_in_Virginia.jpg/250px-2015-09-29_23_37_05_AeroTrain_station_at_the_main_terminal_of_Washington_Dulles_International_Airport_in_Virginia.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2015-09-29_23_37_05_AeroTrain_station_at_the_main_terminal_of_Washington_Dulles_International_Airport_in_Virginia.jpg)

The AeroTrain station in the second basement (2015)

By 2000, there were proposals to renovate the original terminal as part of a $3.4 billion renovation of Dulles Airport.[\[222\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-230)[\[223\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_Daily_Progress_2000-231) Work on the pedestrian tunnel to concourse B was underway,[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Civil_Engineering_2000-45)[\[224\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-232) and several parking garages were being built nearby;[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Civil_Engineering_2000-45)[\[225\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-233) in addition, the terminal's control tower was proposed for replacement.[\[223\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_Daily_Progress_2000-231)[\[226\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-234) An underpass to the new parking garages was completed in 2004 for $81 million,[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Cline_2022-93) and the tunnel to Concourse B also opened that year.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-flydulles.com_1962-9)[\[227\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-235) A 600-foot-long (180 m) tunnel for baggage was developed concurrently,[\[228\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-236) and the Z gates opened in 2005.[\[229\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-237) By the mid-2000s, the MWAA was constructing a security checkpoint,[\[230\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-238)[\[231\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Infanger_2007-239) along with a people mover (by then known as the AeroTrain) leading to the outlying concourses.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Schwartz_p._52-55)[\[231\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Infanger_2007-239) This work was budgeted at $1.3 billion and involved constructing two basement levels below the existing facility, freeing up space on the original upper level.[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-USA_Today_j755-86) The control tower was decommissioned in 2007 after a new control tower opened.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Kelly_j193-54)

The new security checkpoint in the first basement opened in September 2009, replacing all the checkpoints on the upper level; a checkpoint for frequent travelers was retained on the original lower level.[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Yu_2009-88)[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_Washington_Post_2009-89) The AeroTrain station in the second basement opened in early 2010,[\[232\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-RTS2010-240) and the airport's overall expansion was completed the next year.[\[233\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Aratani_i530-241) Additionally, in 2012, checkpoints were added to the Main Terminal as part of the [TSA PreCheck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TSA_PreCheck "TSA PreCheck") frequent-flyer program,[\[234\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-242) and the MWAA began displaying information on security-screening wait times.[\[235\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-243) The Main Terminal gained direct mass-transit access in 2022 with the opening of Washington Metro's Dulles International Airport station,[\[233\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Aratani_i530-241) and an airport lounge sponsored by [Capital One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_One "Capital One") opened there the next year.[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Clabaugh_2023-92)[\[236\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-244) The MWAA announced another master plan for Dulles Airport in 2025.[\[237\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-245)[\[238\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Roussey_2025-246) Renderings of this master plan indicate that a walkway might be built south to midfield concourses A and B.[\[238\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Roussey_2025-246) That December, the [administration of President Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_administration_of_Donald_Trump "Second administration of Donald Trump") solicited proposals for the airport's redevelopment, including potentially expanding or replacing the Main Terminal; although Trump praised the terminal's design at the time, he criticized the airport's overall layout.[\[239\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-247)[\[240\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-248)

[![Image 12: The main terminal as viewed from the west](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b9/Washington_Dulles_International_Airport.jpg/250px-Washington_Dulles_International_Airport.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Washington_Dulles_International_Airport.jpg)

Saarinen had deemed the Dulles Main Terminal "the best thing I have done".[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Kenworthy_n797-27)[\[155\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Baker_1962-163)

When the terminal was being completed in early 1962, the architectural critic [Ada Louise Huxtable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ada_Louise_Huxtable "Ada Louise Huxtable") described Saarinen as having successfully created "a symbolic entrance to the nation", saying that the design had a similar effect to an ancient Greek temple.[\[241\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-249) _[The Baltimore Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Baltimore_Sun "The Baltimore Sun")_ wrote that the terminal's design was "vaguely suggestive of some oriental shrine".[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Sehlstedt_1962-73) Paul J. C. Friedlander, of _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")_, said the swooping roof and slanted glass facade created an effect of "grace and lightness".[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Friedlander_1962-57) The commentator Walter McQuade wrote for _[Architectural Forum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Architectural_Forum "Architectural Forum")_: "It is likely that the most majestic single statement of this integrated expressionism will be his design for Dulles Terminal."[\[242\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-250) Saarinen had deemed the Dulles Main Terminal "the best thing I have done";[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Kenworthy_n797-27)[\[155\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Baker_1962-163) of the projects he had been working on when he died, he had been especially proud of the Dulles terminal and New York's [CBS Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS_Building "CBS Building").[\[243\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-251) Saarinen's wife, the architectural critic [Aline B. Saarinen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aline_B._Saarinen "Aline B. Saarinen"), similarly believed the terminal would be her husband's "best work".[\[244\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-252)

Although the [Associated Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associated_Press "Associated Press") wrote that the completed terminal "was too modern for many tastes when it was built",[\[214\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Danville_Register_and_Bee_1996-222) the [_Architectural Record_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Architectural_Record "Architectural Record") said the building "was almost instantly regarded as a Modern masterpiece".[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Freeman_p._63-31) When the terminal opened, _[Newsday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newsday "Newsday")_ of New York described the building as "definitely a design of the future",[\[155\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Baker_1962-163) and a reporter for the _Baltimore Sun_ said the structure "looks better the closer one gets to it",[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Sehlstedt_1962a-29) _Architectural Forum_, in a 1963 article, wrote that the terminal "happily will never grow into an octopus", referring to the lack of jetways.[\[245\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-253) The [Associated Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associated_Press "Associated Press") wrote that the walls, interior lighting, and control tower combined to create "a dreamlike appearance" at night.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Haughland_1962-2) The architect [Cesar Pelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesar_Pelli "Cesar Pelli"), a former employee of Saarinen's, described the feeling of approaching the Dulles terminal as being similar to that of approaching a "great temple or a great cathedral in the countryside in France".[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Ichniowski_1996-64)

Several commentators described the concave roof as creating a soaring effect,[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Kenworthy_n797-27)[\[246\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-254) and they also likened the building to a plane.[\[163\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-McDowell_p888-171)[\[247\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Howe_1963-255) The [_Bristol Herald Courier_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Herald_Courier "Bristol Herald Courier") said that "no building of such size ever seemed so likely to take flight",[\[163\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-McDowell_p888-171) and a [_Sarasota Journal_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarasota_Journal "Sarasota Journal") writer praised the terminal's beauty, saying: "The trouble is, Mr. Saarinen forgot to put in the engines."[\[247\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Howe_1963-255) [Wolf Von Eckardt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolf_Von_Eckardt "Wolf Von Eckardt") considered the Dulles terminal, along with [Boston City Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_City_Hall "Boston City Hall"), as "the greatest \[building\] on the American scene in a decade or two".[\[248\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-256) Conversely, [Morris Lapidus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Lapidus "Morris Lapidus") wrote for [_Architecture: The AIA Journal_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Architecture:_The_AIA_Journal "Architecture: The AIA Journal") in 1964 that, although the building's exterior was "beautifully bold and daring", the interior lacked scale or embellishing details.[\[249\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-257)

Retrospectively, a commentator for the _[Reporter-Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reporter-Times "Reporter-Times")_ described early reactions as negative, saying that the local and state governments had only reluctantly accepted Saarinen's design.[\[250\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-258) A _New York Times_ article, conversely, characterized the building as having been perceived "as a bold reflection of American aviation" from the outset.[\[251\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-259) In 1977, when the terminal's expansion was first being considered, a _Washington Post_ writer deemed the terminal Dulles Airport's "one great strength", saying it "looks far more capable of flight" than ordinary aircraft.[\[176\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Morris_1977-184) Upon the terminal's 20th anniversary in 1982, _The New York Times_ wrote that it was "considered by many to be a landmark of 20th-century design".[\[252\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-260) _The Washington Post_ referred to the terminal in 1989 as "inspiring from afar and maddening from within" because of the overcrowding inside.[\[253\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-261) A writer for [_The Wilson Quarterly_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wilson_Quarterly "The Wilson Quarterly") wrote in 1995 that the Dulles Main Terminal and the [TWA Flight Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TWA_Flight_Center "TWA Flight Center") demonstrated how Saarinen "push\[ed\] design beyond the confines of the Modern Movement".[\[254\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-262)

A writer for _The New York Times_ said in 2003 that the Dulles Airport Main Terminal, like Saarinen's nearly-contemporary [North Christian Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Christian_Church "North Christian Church"), "immediately seizes even the casual onlooker's eye with its dramatic shape and carries it heavenward".[\[255\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-263) The next year, the writer Mark Gottdiener praised the exterior as a "dramatic, austere statement" but said that the interior, particularly the inefficiency of the mobile lounges, was inadequate.[\[104\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Gottdiener_2001-112) A 2006 book about Saarinen's architecture said that his design "gave structure an expressive dimension".[\[256\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-264) Roger K. Lewis wrote in 2010 that the terminal had aged well over the years, not only because the interiors were so easily adaptable to different uses, but also because the terminal's design was simple yet memorable.[\[257\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-265) Over the years, the building's design has also evoked comparisons to birds.[\[258\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-266)

### Awards and architectural influence

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Awards and architectural influence")\]

The [Greater Washington Board of Trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Washington_Board_of_Trade "Greater Washington Board of Trade") gave the terminal building an award for its design in 1964,[\[259\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-267) and Saarinen's firm received an honor award from the [American Institute of Architects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Institute_of_Architects "American Institute of Architects") (AIA) in 1966 for the terminal's design.[\[260\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-268)[\[261\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-269) A 1976 poll of American architects ranked it the country's third-best design, tied with [Fallingwater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fallingwater "Fallingwater"),[\[262\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-270) and one of the most impactful buildings constructed in the U.S. since the [American Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolution "American Revolution").[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Ames_v927-35) The Dulles Main Terminal won the AIA's [Twenty-five Year Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twenty-five_Year_Award "Twenty-five Year Award") in 1988.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-A-1988-05-26) The [United States Postal Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Postal_Service "United States Postal Service") issued a stamp depicting the terminal in 1982 to honor Saarinen's designs,[\[263\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Tower_j689-271) and the terminal was also included in the 2013 [PBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PBS "PBS") documentary and companion book _[10 Buildings that Changed America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10_That_Changed_America "10 That Changed America")_.[\[264\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-272)

When the terminal was first expanded in the 1970s, there were calls for the Dulles Main Terminal to be added to the [National Register of Historic Places](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Register_of_Historic_Places "National Register of Historic Places") (NRHP).[\[174\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Huxtable_o904-182)[\[265\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-273) This would have made it one of the youngest-ever NRHP listings,[\[173\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Hodge_1977-181) as most NRHP sites cannot be listed until they are at least fifty years old.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Ames_v927-35) The FAA opposed the NRHP designation, as it would have subjected any potential renovations to a lengthy approval process.[\[173\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Hodge_1977-181) The terminal was deemed eligible for NRHP listing in 1978, on the merits of its design.[\[266\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-274) Ultimately, it was never added to the NRHP because of the FAA's concerns that such a designation would disrupt airport operations.[\[267\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-275)[\[i\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-276)

When the midfield terminals at Dulles Airport were developed, they were built of glass and metal to avoid drawing attention away from the Main Terminal's concrete structure.[\[268\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-277) The original terminal at [Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwan_Taoyuan_International_Airport "Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport") in Taoyuan, Taiwan, was modeled after Dulles Airport's Main Terminal;[\[269\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-278)[\[270\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-279) the buildings were so visually similar that the [Taiwanese government once erroneously printed passports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwan_passport#Dulles_Airport_image_incident "Taiwan passport") depicting the Dulles Main Terminal.[\[271\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-280) Other airport terminals drew comparison to the Dulles Main Terminal, including the former passenger terminal at [Montréal–Mirabel International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montr%C3%A9al%E2%80%93Mirabel_International_Airport "Montréal–Mirabel International Airport")[\[272\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-281) and Terminal 2 at [San Diego International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Diego_International_Airport "San Diego International Airport").[\[273\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-282)[\[274\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-283)

![Image 1](https://www.ashburnmagazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/Metropolitan-Washington-Airports-Authority3-678x381.jpg)

**GROOVY RIDE**
---------------

**By Chris Wadsworth**

Jyrki Ihanainen’s first trip to the United States was in 1985. He flew from his native Finland to Dulles International Airport. When the giant 747 landed, Ihanainen thought it was puzzling that the plane didn’t pull up to a gate. And it was even more puzzling when a strange, bus-like vehicle parked next to the plane, the passengers got on board, and it drove them to the main terminal.

“We had transferred at London Heathrow — which at the time was the most advanced airport in the world,” Ihanainen said. “So when we got to Dulles and I saw the people mover, I was like, ‘What the heck, did we just arrive in the Stone Age?’ I thought it was pretty funny.”

That day, Ihanainen took his first ride on Dulles’ famous mobile lounges — an experience the Broadlands resident has repeated hundreds of times since as he travels around the world for work and pleasure.

[![Image 2](http://www.ashburnmagazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/Metropolitan-Washington-Airports-Authority5-1024x806.jpg)](http://www.ashburnmagazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/Metropolitan-Washington-Airports-Authority5.jpg)

The odd, ungainly vehicles were part of Eero Saarinen’s original vision of Dulles when the Finnish-American architect designed it in the early 1960s. Commercial air travel was growing, and the tiny airports of old — where propeller planes pulled right up to a single, small terminal building — were fading away. Airports were getting bigger, and Saarinen created the mobile lounges as a way to help passengers avoid long walks from the entrance and ticket counters to planes.

[![Image 3](http://www.ashburnmagazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/2-6.jpg)](http://www.ashburnmagazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/2-6.jpg)

“It was the start of the jet age,” said Micah Lillard, public information officer for the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority. “Commercial air traffic was growing. You had more and more planes trying to take up a very small amount of space outside the terminal. As more started coming, you had to find parking spots in remote places. The people movers were an efficient way to get people out to these remote spots.”

[![Image 4](http://www.ashburnmagazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/Metropolitan-Washington-Airports-Authority2.jpg)](http://www.ashburnmagazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/Metropolitan-Washington-Airports-Authority2.jpg)

The mobile lounges were originally envisioned as just that — elegant waiting rooms on wheels. Passengers would arrive at Dulles’ stunning soaring main terminal, check in at the ticket counters and then walk right into one of his moving lounges. The experience was supposed to be like a hip salon — with stylish furnishings and even cocktails to sip as the people mover — another nickname for the lounges — transported you directly to your plane. There, they would raise and lower to meet the doorway of the plane.

Unfortunately, the reality never quite matched the dream. Air travel and airports grew faster than anyone anticipated. The arrival of large jumbo jets meant far more passengers than the people movers could handle, and the sheer number of airlines and airplanes meant that giant, winding airports with multiple arms or piers extending out became the norm.

[![Image 5](http://www.ashburnmagazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/Metropolitan-Washington-Airports-Authority7.jpg)](http://www.ashburnmagazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/Metropolitan-Washington-Airports-Authority7.jpg)

Still, Dulles and a handful of other airports around the world used the people movers for years, even if the elegance and the cocktails never quite materialized. They have been phased out nearly everywhere today — replaced by trains, moving sidewalks and even buses. Indeed, Dulles launched an underground train service to its terminals in 2010. But Concourse D isn’t connected to the train, and a small fleet of people movers — about three dozen — continues to whisk passengers back and forth from the main terminal during a typical day.

[![Image 6](http://www.ashburnmagazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/image-2.jpg)](http://www.ashburnmagazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/image-2.jpg)

“We find that a lot of aviation enthusiasts enjoy them,” Lillard said. “They get to see a perspective for spotting planes that most people don’t get to see.”

In fact, during its annual Dulles Day Plane Pull event, the airport offers visitors a tour of the runways on one of the people movers.

[![Image 7](http://www.ashburnmagazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/Library-of-Congress1-1009x1024.png)](http://www.ashburnmagazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/Library-of-Congress1.png)

Aviation enthusiasts aside, many passengers might find standing in the crowded people movers and waiting for them to start a bit of a drag — a far cry from the charming, relaxed experience Saarinen envisioned. But for his fellow countryman Jyrki Ihanainen, it’s a fun and efficient throwback to the Dulles International of the past.

“They’re a little old-fashioned, sure, but they operate them very well, even during peak times. They run every five minutes and it’s easy in, easy out,” he said. “I don’t mind them at all.”

[![Image 8](http://www.ashburnmagazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/Metropolitan-Washington-Airports-Authority1.jpg)](http://www.ashburnmagazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/Metropolitan-Washington-Airports-Authority1.jpg)

_(Archive images courtesy of the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority)_

\===============

Mobile Lounges versus Plane-Mates
---------------------------------

There are actually two different types of people movers — the “mobile lounges” and the “Plane-Mates.” The mobile lounges are used primarily between terminals for domestic passengers, while the Plane-Mates — which also shuttle between terminals — can also be used to off-load passengers directly from planes. You can tell the difference between the two by the “smokestack” like appendages on top of the Plane-Mates.

[![Image 9](http://www.ashburnmagazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/Metropolitan-Washington-Airports-Authority4.jpg)](http://www.ashburnmagazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/Metropolitan-Washington-Airports-Authority4.jpg)

And if you are a true history buff, you will love this 1958 concept video that shows how air travel was changing and why Dulles International is designed the way it is. It’s very cool.

| | | | Location | | --- | | [![Image 27: Map](https://maps.wikimedia.org/img/osm-intl,15,38.955833333333,-77.447777777778,270x200.png?lang=en&domain=en.wikipedia.org&title=Dulles_International_Airport_station&revid=1328056077&groups=_8b6b65fab83a78bdb9746bc699c9d45e31a58888&parser=legacy)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Map/15/38.955833333333/-77.447777777778/en) | | **Washington Dulles International Airport station** (commonly **Dulles International Airport** or **Dulles Airport**) is a [Washington Metro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Metro "Washington Metro") station at [Dulles International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport "Dulles International Airport") in [Loudoun County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loudoun_County,_Virginia "Loudoun County, Virginia"), [Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia "Virginia"), U.S., on the [Silver Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_Line_/(Washington_Metro/) "Silver Line (Washington Metro)"). After years of delays,[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_station#cite_note-dulles_station-2)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_station#cite_note-Aratani_2015-3)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_station#cite_note-4) the station opened on November 15, 2022. The station was originally planned to be underground[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_station#cite_note-dulles_station-2) but was built as an above-ground station next to daily parking garage 1.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_station#cite_note-5) The station is connected to the [Main Terminal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal "Dulles International Airport Main Terminal") using the existing pedestrian tunnel which connects the hourly and daily parking lots and parking garage 1 to the baggage claim level of the airport terminal; the tunnel is equipped with [moving sidewalks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moving_walkway "Moving walkway"). A Washington Metro station had been considered for Dulles since at least 1969. A 1971 engineering study suggested an underground station, with the top of the rail 28 feet (8.5 m) below a [parking lot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parking_lot "Parking lot").[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_station#cite_note-6)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_station#cite_note-Dulles_station-7) Formal plans were not made until 2002, with the first phase of the project commencing in 2004. The Silver Line was developed in the 21st century to link [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."), by rail to [Dulles International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport "Dulles International Airport") and the [edge cities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edge_city "Edge city") of [Tysons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tysons,_Virginia "Tysons, Virginia"), [Reston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reston,_Virginia "Reston, Virginia"), [Herndon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herndon,_Virginia "Herndon, Virginia"), and [Ashburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashburn,_Virginia "Ashburn, Virginia").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_station#cite_note-8) It was built in two phases; the first phase, linking Washington, D.C., to [Wiehle–Reston East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiehle%E2%80%93Reston_East_station "Wiehle–Reston East station"), opened in 2014.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_station#cite_note-9) [![Image 28: Dulles Metro Station](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/17/Dulles_Metro_Station.jpg/250px-Dulles_Metro_Station.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dulles_Metro_Station.jpg) The Dulles Metro Station under construction in November 2013. The funding and planning of Phase 2 through Dulles Airport continued while Phase 1 was being constructed. On April 6, 2011, the [Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Washington_Airports_Authority "Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority") (MWAA) board voted 9–4 to build an underground station 550 feet (170 m) away from the terminal, rather than an above-ground station 1,150 feet (350 m) away from the terminal, at an additional cost of $330 million. Construction of the underground station would have extended its expected opening to mid-2017.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_station#cite_note-10) However, on July 20, 2011, the MWAA board reversed its previous vote and approved an above-ground station due to pressure from state and local officials to reduce overall project costs.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_station#cite_note-11) In 2012, the [Loudoun County Board of Supervisors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loudoun_County_Board_of_Supervisors "Loudoun County Board of Supervisors") voted 5 to 4 to extend the line to Dulles Airport and into the county.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_station#cite_note-12) On April 25, 2013, the Phase 2 contract was issued at a cost of $1.177 billion.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_station#cite_note-13) The originally planned single-side platform station would not meet current Metro specifications for a center platform, which is necessary since current plans would extend service beyond the airport to western suburbs. Plans for an above-ground facility drew concerns from the Virginia Historic Preservation Office regarding the visual impact on the [Eero Saarinen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eero_Saarinen "Eero Saarinen")\-designed terminal. Consultants estimated that an above-ground station would save $640 million in construction costs.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_station#cite_note-14) The pedestrian tunnel connecting the terminal and daily and hourly lots to parking garage 1 was closed in January 2016 in order to reconfigure that tunnel section to accommodate the future Metro station entrance.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_station#cite_note-dulles_station-2) The pedestrian tunnel was reopened in November 2018.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_station#cite_note-15) In April 2015, project officials pushed back the opening date for the station to late 2019, stating that stricter requirements for stormwater management caused much of the delay. Per officials, the line also had to incorporate improvements to the system's automated train controls that were a late addition to the project's first phase.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_station#cite_note-16) In August 2019, project officials reported that they expected construction on the second phase of the Silver Line to be completed by mid-2020.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_station#cite_note-17) The opening date was postponed to early 2021,[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_station#cite_note-18) then to late 2021.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_station#cite_note-19) In February 2021, Metro announced that it would need five months to test the Phase 2 extension.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_station#cite_note-20)[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_station#cite_note-21) The MWAA then announced that the Phase 2 extension should be substantially complete by Labor Day 2021,[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_station#cite_note-22) although MWAA subsequently missed this deadline.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_station#cite_note-23) MWAA declared the work on the rail line to be "substantially complete" in November 2021. However, WMATA estimated that it could take five months of testing and other preparations before passenger service could begin.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_station#cite_note-04nov2021-24) Simulated service testing began operating along the Phase 2 tracks in October 2022.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_station#cite_note-25)[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_station#cite_note-26)[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_station#cite_note-27) Phase 2 formally opened on November 15, 2022.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_station#cite_note-nov15-28)[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_station#cite_note-29) 1. **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_station#cite_ref-Data_1-0)** ["Metrorail Ridership Summary"](https://www.wmata.com/initiatives/ridership-portal/Metrorail-Ridership-Summary.cfm).
